title: The Thirty Years' War
titleline: The Thirty Years' War - The History Web
para1: The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) began in Bohemia, where the Protestant estates feared the Catholic Habsburg succession would revoke their religious liberties, guaranteed by the Letter of Majesty of 1609. In May 1618 Bohemian nobles threw two imperial governors from a window of Prague Castle, the Defenestration of Prague, and set up a rebel state, crowning the Calvinist Frederick V of the Palatinate 'the Winter King'. The Catholic League and Spain crushed the revolt at the White Mountain (1620), and the Palatinate itself was conquered, turning a Bohemian rebellion into a European war as Denmark, then Sweden, then France intervened against the Habsburgs.
para2: Under Emperor Ferdinand II the Catholic powers nearly won outright. Wallenstein's imperial armies and Tilly's Leaguers defeated the Danes at Lutter (1626) and drove them from the war (Peace of Lubeck, 1629), and the Edict of Restitution (1629) ordered Protestant lands confiscated since 1552 returned to the church. The overreach provoked Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, financed by France, to intervene: his reformed army smashed Tilly at Breitenfeld (1631), swept through Germany, and fell at Lutzen (1632) even in victory. After Wallenstein's assassination in 1634, imperial arms recovered at Nordlingen, but in 1635 Catholic France declared war on Spain openly, and the conflict became a general struggle for the mastery of Europe.
para3: The last thirteen years were the most devastating. Armies of all sides, paid late or never, lived off the land, plundering, burning and spreading famine and plague across Germany. Swedish victory at Wittstock (1636), French victory at Rocroi over the Spanish infantry (1643), and the devastation of regions like the Palatinate and Magdeburg, sacked in 1631 with the loss of most of its people, made the war a byword for horror. Germany lost perhaps a quarter to a third of its population, some regions far more, and the economy of the Holy Roman Empire was set back generations.
para4: Exhaustion brought the Peace of Westphalia (1648), negotiated at Munster and Osnabruck. The settlement confirmed the near-sovereignty of the Empire's princes, including their right to foreign alliances, recognized Calvinism alongside Catholicism and Lutheranism, and awarded Sweden western Pomerania and France lands in Alsace; Switzerland and the Dutch Republic were recognized as independent. Westphalia is conventionally taken to found the European order of sovereign states: it ended the ideal of a unified Christian empire, made France the leading continental power, weakened Habsburg Spain decisively, and established that religious uniformity would no longer decide international politics.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Thirty Years' War

title: The English Civil War and the Protectorate
titleline: The English Civil War and the Protectorate - The History Web
para1: The English Civil War (1642-1651) grew from the breakdown of trust between Charles I and his Parliaments. Charles ruled eleven years without Parliament (1629-1640), raising money by disputed prerogative levies like ship money, while his archbishop, William Laud, imposed ceremonial conformity on the church. When Charles tried to force a new prayer book on Presbyterian Scotland, the Scots rebelled, occupied northern England, and forced him to call Parliament. The Long Parliament (1640) impeached his ministers, abolished prerogative courts, and, after the Irish Catholic revolt of 1641 raised the question of who could be trusted with an army, split between Royalists ('Cavaliers') and Parliamentarians ('Roundheads'). Charles raised his standard at Nottingham in August 1642.
para2: The first war was indecisive until Parliament created the New Model Army (1645), a professional force under Fairfax and Cromwell that destroyed the king's main army at Naseby (1645). Charles surrendered to the Scots, who handed him to Parliament. His secret dealings, and a Scottish invasion on his behalf, provoked the Second Civil War (1648); Cromwell crushed it at Preston, and the army purged Parliament and tried the king. Charles I was executed on 30 January 1649 outside Whitehall, an event that shocked Europe. England was declared a republic, the Commonwealth, while Cromwell's army conquered Ireland, the storming of Drogheda and Wexford with their massacres, and crushed the Scots at Dunbar (1650) and Worcester (1651), where the future Charles II barely escaped.
para3: The Commonwealth's experiments ended in military rule. Cromwell expelled the Rump Parliament in 1653, and after the failure of the Nominated Assembly he accepted the Instrument of Government, becoming Lord Protector. The Protectorate (1653-1658) governed through written constitution, major-generals and a tolerant Protestant church settlement, while Cromwell fought a successful war against Spain, taking Jamaica, and made England a respected power again. Yet the regime rested on the army and on Cromwell's person; Parliament and Protector repeatedly clashed, and republicans, Levellers and Fifth Monarchists all denounced him as a usurper.
para4: Cromwell died in September 1658. His son Richard lasted months before the army deposed him, and in the chaos General George Monck marched from Scotland, restored the surviving members of the Long Parliament, and arranged free elections. In May 1660 Charles II was invited home and the monarchy restored, but the republican decade could not be undone: no English king ever again ruled without Parliament, the New Model's professionalism endured, and the memory of 1649 shaped the constitutional settlement of 1688-1689 and the later British state.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: English Civil Wars

title: The Glorious Revolution
titleline: The Glorious Revolution - The History Web
para1: The Glorious Revolution (1688-1689) replaced the Catholic James II of England with his Protestant daughter Mary and her husband William III of Orange, and settled the English constitution on parliamentary terms. James, succeeding his brother Charles II in 1685, alienated the political nation within three years: he suspended the Test Acts by royal prerogative, kept a standing army near London, promoted Catholics to office, and prosecuted seven bishops who petitioned against his religious policy. The birth of a son, and Catholic heir, in June 1688 ended hopes that his rule was a temporary Catholic interlude, and seven leading Englishmen invited William, stadtholder of the Dutch Republic, to intervene.
para2: William landed at Torbay on 5 November 1688 with a Dutch army of some 15,000, claiming to defend England's religion and liberties and to call a free Parliament. James's army, larger but unreliable, melted as officers and even his daughter Anne deserted; James attempted flight, was allowed to escape to France, and the revolution was effected with almost no fighting in England, though it took real wars to impose in Scotland and Ireland, where the Jacobites were defeated at the Boyne (1690) and Aughrim (1691).
para3: In January 1689 the Convention Parliament declared that James, by fleeing, had abdicated, and offered the crown jointly to William and Mary. The offer came with conditions: the Declaration of Right, enacted as the Bill of Rights (1689), condemned James's abuses and laid down that no monarch could suspend laws, tax without Parliament, maintain a standing army in peacetime without consent, or interfere with elections and parliamentary speech; and it barred Catholics, or anyone married to a Catholic, from the throne. The Toleration Act (1689) gave limited freedom to Protestant dissenters, and the Mutiny Act and annual supply made Parliament a permanent part of government.
para4: The revolution's consequences reached far. In Britain it established parliamentary monarchy, party politics, and the financial revolution, the Bank of England (1694) and a funded national debt, that underwrote Britain's wars and empire. Internationally it brought England into William's Grand Alliance against Louis XIV, beginning the 'Second Hundred Years' War' between Britain and France. In political thought, John Locke's Two Treatises justified government by consent and resistance to tyranny, feeding later liberalism, while Jacobitism, the claim of James's line, kept rebellion alive in Scotland until Culloden (1746). 'Glorious' meant, above all, bloodless and lawful: a revolution made to look like no revolution at all.

title: The War of the Spanish Succession
titleline: The War of the Spanish Succession - The History Web
para1: The War of the Spanish Succession (1701-1714) decided who would inherit the vast empire of the last Spanish Habsburg, Charles II: Spain itself, the Spanish Netherlands, most of Italy, and colonies from the Caribbean to the Pacific. Charles died childless in 1700, leaving his crown by will to Philip of Anjou, grandson of Louis XIV of France. The Austrian Habsburgs claimed it for the Archduke Charles. Louis's acceptance for his grandson, and his provocations, recognizing the Stuart pretender, seizing the Spanish Netherlands' barrier fortresses, and monopolizing American trade, drove Britain, the Dutch Republic and Austria into the Grand Alliance, fearing a Bourbon super-state.
para2: The war was fought on five fronts. In the Low Countries and Germany, the Duke of Marlborough won a string of victories unmatched in British military history: Blenheim (1704), which saved Vienna and destroyed the Franco-Bavarian army; Ramillies (1706), which conquered the Spanish Netherlands in a day; Oudenarde (1708); and the Pyrrhic Malplaquet (1709). In Spain the Allies landed the Archduke Charles as 'Charles III', twice took Madrid but could not hold it, and were broken at Almansa (1707) and Brihuega-Villaviciosa (1710), leaving Philip V master of the Spanish heartland. At sea, Britain took Gibraltar (1704) and Minorca (1708), and in the north the war merged with the Great Northern War's diplomacy.
para3: Exhaustion, famine in France's terrible winter of 1709, and political change ended the war. In Britain the Tories, hostile to continental war, won power in 1710 and dismissed Marlborough; and when the Archduke Charles unexpectedly became Emperor Charles VI in 1711, British opinion refused to trade a Bourbon Spain for a Habsburg one. Britain negotiated separately, and the Treaties of Utrecht (1713) and Rastatt and Baden (1714) settled the peace: Philip V kept Spain and the Indies, renouncing the French succession for himself and his line; Austria took the Spanish Netherlands and most of Spanish Italy, with Sicily going to Savoy; Britain kept Gibraltar and Minorca and won the asiento, the contract to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish America.
para4: Utrecht redrew Europe. The Spanish Empire was partitioned, the balance of power became the explicit principle of European diplomacy, and Britain emerged as the great naval and commercial winner. France was humbled but not broken, Austria gained a new Italian empire it could barely defend, and the Dutch barrier against France was entrenched. Spain, meanwhile, remained under the Bourbon dynasty Philip founded, which reformed the state along French lines and rules Spain to the present day, with interruptions.
source1label: Britannica: War of the Spanish Succession
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: War of the Spanish Succession

title: The Seven Years' War
titleline: The Seven Years' War - The History Web
para1: The Seven Years' War (1756-1763) was the first truly global war, fought in Europe, North America, India, the Caribbean and the Pacific. Its immediate cause in Europe was the 'diplomatic revolution' of 1756: centuries of Franco-Habsburg rivalry ended in an alliance between Austria and France, joined by Russia, to crush Prussia, whose king Frederick II had seized Silesia from Maria Theresa of Austria in 1740. Britain aligned with Prussia, subsidizing Frederick while fighting France for empire overseas. Frederick struck first, invading Saxony in 1756 to forestall the coalition against him.
para2: Frederick's Prussia survived by generalship against encircling enemies four times its size. In 1757 he destroyed a French and imperial army at Rossbach in under an hour and a month later routed the Austrians at Leuthen; but the Russians won at Gross-Jagersdorf and Kunersdorf (1759), where the Prussian army was annihilated and Frederick contemplated suicide, and Austrian and Russian armies briefly occupied Berlin (1760). The 'miracle of the House of Brandenburg' came in 1762 when the pro-Prussian Peter III succeeded Elizabeth in Russia, made peace, and even returned conquests; Sweden then dropped out, and Austria, bankrupted, made peace at Hubertusburg (1763), restoring the status quo: Prussia kept Silesia and emerged confirmed as a great power.
para3: In North America, where the war had effectively begun in 1754 with skirmishes in the Ohio valley, France initially prevailed, but British money, sea power and colonial manpower turned the tide: Louisbourg fell in 1758, and in 1759 Wolfe defeated Montcalm on the Plains of Abraham outside Quebec, both generals dying, and Montreal surrendered in 1760, ending New France. In India, Robert Clive's victory at Plassey (1757) made the East India Company master of Bengal, and Pondicherry fell in 1761. Spain, entering late on France's side, lost Havana and Manila to British expeditions in 1762.
para4: The Peace of Paris (1763) redrew the world map: France ceded Canada and all territory east of the Mississippi to Britain and Louisiana to Spain, and left India reduced to a few trading posts; Spain ceded Florida and received Louisiana and Havana back. Britain became the dominant colonial and naval power, and the costs of victory, taxing the American colonies to pay the war's debt, set in train the crisis that produced the American Revolution a decade later. In Europe the war confirmed Prussia's survival and Russia's arrival as a decisive player, and it left Austria and France nursing debts and grievances that would surface again in the revolutionary era.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Seven Years' War

title: The Congress of Vienna and the Restoration
titleline: The Congress of Vienna and the Restoration - The History Web
para1: The Congress of Vienna (September 1814 - June 1815) was the great peace conference that rebuilt Europe after more than twenty years of Revolutionary and Napoleonic war. Nearly every state and court of Europe sent representatives to the Austrian capital, where the Austrian foreign minister Metternich, Britain's Castlereagh, Prussia's Hardenberg, Russia's Tsar Alexander I, and, most skillfully, France's Talleyrand, representing the defeated power, bargained over the map while the city danced. The guiding principles were legitimacy, restoring the old dynasties Napoleon had displaced, the balance of power, so no state could again dominate Europe, and compensation for the victors' losses and efforts.
para2: The territorial settlement redrew the continent. France returned roughly to its 1792 borders. To contain it, the Dutch Republic and the Austrian Netherlands were merged into a Kingdom of the Netherlands, Prussia received the Rhineland, and Austria kept Lombardy and Venetia. Austria and Prussia were compensated in Italy and Germany for the Polish lands lost to Russia, which kept most of Napoleon's Grand Duchy of Warsaw as 'Congress Poland'. The Holy Roman Empire, dissolved in 1806, was not restored; instead thirty-nine German states formed a loose German Confederation under Austrian presidency. Sweden kept Norway, taken from Denmark, and Britain kept Malta, the Cape of Good Hope and Ceylon.
para3: The negotiations were interrupted in March 1815 by Napoleon's escape from Elba and his Hundred Days, which ended at Waterloo in June; the second Treaty of Paris (1815) then imposed harsher terms on France, an indemnity and an army of occupation. To preserve the settlement, Alexander I promoted the Holy Alliance of Christian monarchs, while Austria, Prussia, Russia and Britain formed the Quadruple Alliance, pledging to meet in congresses to maintain the peace, the beginning of the 'Congress System' at Aix-la-Chapelle, Troppau and Laibach.
para4: The Vienna settlement gave Europe nearly forty years without a general war, an achievement no previous peace had matched. Its conservative order, defended by Metternich's Carlsbad Decrees and occasional interventions, suppressed the liberal and national movements the revolutionary era had unleashed, but only until they burst out in 1830 and 1848. Belgium seceded from the Netherlands in 1830, and German and Italian unification later demolished the map, yet the balance-of-power system Vienna created, and the idea of settling affairs by congress diplomacy, shaped European statecraft to 1914 and beyond.

title: The Revolutions of 1848
titleline: The Revolutions of 1848 - The History Web
para1: The Revolutions of 1848 were a wave of uprisings that swept across Europe, the most widespread revolutionary year in its history. Behind them lay economic crisis, the potato blight and harvest failures of 1845-1847, industrial slump and unemployment, combined with demands for constitutions, national independence and, in the west, wider suffrage. The spark came in France: in February 1848 the 'banquet campaign' against Louis-Philippe's corruption brought down the July Monarchy in three days of Paris barricades, and the Second Republic was proclaimed, with national workshops for the unemployed and universal male suffrage.
para2: The fire spread within weeks. In Vienna, students and workers drove Metternich himself into exile (March 1848); Hungary under Kossuth won a constitution from the frightened emperor; Czechs, Croats, Romanians and Italians of the empire asserted their own national claims. In Berlin, Frederick William IV of Prussia, after street fighting, promised a constitution, and a German National Assembly gathered in Frankfurt to write one for a united Germany. In Italy, Milan expelled the Austrians in the Five Days, Venice declared a republic, and Piedmont-Sardinia went to war for Italian independence, while the pope fled Rome, where Mazzini's Roman Republic was proclaimed in 1849.
para3: The revolutions then divided and were crushed one by one. In France, the June Days (1848) saw the army and provincial militias massacre the Parisian workers after the workshops were closed, and in December Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte was elected president, ending as emperor in 1852. In the Habsburg lands, the army retook Vienna (October 1848) and Prague, the new emperor Franz Joseph abolished the March constitution, and Hungary's full declaration of independence was destroyed in 1849 by Austrian and Russian armies, Russia intervening to save the monarchy. The Frankfurt Parliament, after a year of debate, offered the German crown to Frederick William IV, who refused to 'pick up a crown from the gutter'; the assembly dissolved, and Prussian troops finished off the last risings. In Italy, Austria defeated Piedmont at Custoza (1848) and Novara (1849), and France restored the pope by taking Rome.
para4: The revolutions failed almost everywhere in their immediate aims, but 1848 changed Europe permanently. Serfdom was abolished for good in the Austrian Empire; universal male suffrage, though abused, had come to France; constitutions survived in Prussia and Piedmont; and the movements for German and Italian unity learned to look not to assemblies but to 'blood and iron' and Cavour's diplomacy, achieving within a generation by war and statecraft what the revolutionaries of 1848 could not. Marx and Engels, whose Communist Manifesto appeared as the revolutions began, drew the lesson that would feed the socialist movements of the next century.

title: The Crimean War
titleline: The Crimean War - The History Web
para1: The Crimean War (1853-1856) pitted Russia against the Ottoman Empire, France, Britain and eventually Sardinia-Piedmont, the only great-power war in Europe between 1815 and 1914. Its immediate quarrel was almost farcical, rival rights of Catholic and Orthodox monks over the Holy Places in Jerusalem, but the substance was the 'Eastern Question': Tsar Nicholas I claimed a protectorate over the Ottoman Empire's Orthodox Christians and expected its collapse, while France championed the Catholics and Britain was determined to block Russian expansion toward the Mediterranean. When the Ottomans refused his demands, Nicholas occupied the Danubian Principalities (Moldavia and Wallachia) in 1853, and the Ottoman Empire declared war after Russia destroyed its fleet at Sinope (November 1853).
para2: France and Britain entered in March 1854, and after Austria's pressure forced Russia to evacuate the principalities, the allies decided to strike at Russia's naval power itself: they landed in Crimea in September 1854 to take Sevastopol, home of the Black Sea Fleet. The war's battles became legends of mismanagement and endurance: the Alma (September 1854), a bloody allied victory; Balaclava (October 1854), with the thin red line of Highlanders and the disastrous Charge of the Light Brigade, a cavalry attack misdirected into a valley of guns; and Inkerman (November 1854), the 'soldiers' battle' in the fog, after which the allies, unprepared for winter, nearly died of cold, hunger and disease in their camps.
para3: The siege of Sevastopol lasted nearly a year, its earthworks and artillery foreshadowing industrial siege warfare. The public storm over conditions, exposed by the first great war correspondents like William Howard Russell of The Times, brought down the Aberdeen government in Britain, and Florence Nightingale's nursing mission at Scutari cut the horrific death rate from disease and founded modern nursing. Sardinia joined the allies in 1855 to win a seat at the peace table for the Italian cause. After the fall of the Malakoff redoubt (September 1855) the Russians blew up Sevastopol's remaining forts and evacuated; the accession of Alexander II, after Nicholas I died in March 1855, opened the way to peace.
para4: By the Treaty of Paris (1856) the Black Sea was neutralized, forbidding Russian warships and bases, a humiliation Russia nursed until it repudiated the clause in 1870, and the Ottoman Empire was admitted to the European concert with guarantees of its integrity. The war's costs, some 750,000 dead, mostly of disease, and shattered finances, drove Russia's great reforms, above all the emancipation of the serfs (1861). It ended the post-1815 conservative solidarity of Russia and Austria, leaving Austria isolated when the wars of Italian and German unification came, and it announced modern war: railways, telegraphs, rifled muskets, trench lines and war photography had all arrived.

title: The Swedish Empire
titleline: The Swedish Empire - The History Web
para1: The Swedish Empire, the stormaktstiden or 'age of great power', made Sweden the dominant power of the Baltic in the seventeenth century. Its foundations were laid under Gustavus Vasa, who broke the Kalmar Union in 1523, seized church wealth in the Reformation, and built a centralized monarchy, and by the conquests of his grandsons in the eastern Baltic. The empire proper began with Gustavus Adolphus (1611-1632): reformed army, national conscription, mobile artillery, and battlefield drill made Sweden's army the most modern in Europe. His intervention in the Thirty Years' War, from the victory of Breitenfeld (1631) to his death at Lutzen (1632), made Sweden the arbiter of Germany.
para2: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) rewarded Sweden with western Pomerania, Bremen-Verden and Wismar, giving it control of the mouths of the Oder, Elbe and Weser. Under Charles X Gustav, Sweden seized Scania, Halland and Blekinge from Denmark (Treaty of Roskilde, 1658), closing the Danish strait empire, and under Charles XI the realm was consolidated: the reduction of 1680 expropriated the great nobles' crown lands, financing a standing army and the allotment system, indelningsverket, that quartered soldiers on farms. The Baltic had become a Swedish lake, and the empire stretched from Norway to Estonia and Ingria.
para3: Charles XI's son Charles XII inherited the empire in 1697 at fifteen, and the neighbors he had humbled, Denmark, Saxony-Poland and Peter the Great's Russia, attacked in 1700 to recover their losses. The young king's response was astonishing: he knocked Denmark out at once, annihilated a far larger Russian army at Narva (1700), then spent six years conquering Poland and Saxony, deposing Augustus the Strong. But in 1709, deep in Ukraine, his army was destroyed at Poltava, and the empire collapsed around him: Russia occupied the Baltic provinces, Hanover and Prussia took the German lands, and Charles, returning from Turkish exile, was killed besieging Fredriksten in 1718. The treaties of Stockholm and Nystad (1720-1721) stripped Sweden of everything except Finland and part of Pomerania.
para4: The empire's fall made Sweden a minor power and Russia the new master of the Baltic. At home, the death of Charles XII ended royal absolutism and opened the Age of Liberty (1719-1772), a remarkable experiment in parliamentary party government under the Hats and Caps, ended by Gustav III's coup. Sweden lost Finland to Russia in 1809, gained Norway in compensation in 1814, and, under Bernadotte, adopted the neutrality it has largely kept since. The stormaktstiden remained Sweden's national myth: proof that a poor country of barely a million people could, by military organization and state discipline, briefly rule an empire.

title: The Cossack Hetmanate
titleline: The Cossack Hetmanate - The History Web
para1: The Cossack Hetmanate was the semi-autonomous Cossack state that ruled central Ukraine for over a century after the uprising of Bohdan Khmelnytsky in 1648. Its roots lay in the Zaporozhian Cossacks, the self-governing warrior host 'beyond the rapids' of the Dnieper, runaway serfs, frontiersmen and freebooters who raided the Crimean Khanate and the Ottoman Black Sea, and who chafed under Polish-Lithuanian rule that treated them as a resource to be registered and limited. Tensions over noble encroachment, the curbing of the Cossack register, and the persecution of the Orthodox faith in the Commonwealth's borderlands exploded in 1648, when Khmelnytsky, wronged by a Polish official, allied with the Crimean Tatars and destroyed two Polish armies at Zhovti Vody and Korsun.
para2: The revolt became a war of liberation that redrew eastern Europe. Khmelnytsky's armies, swollen by peasants, swept the Commonwealth's eastern lands in upheavals that included massacres of Polish nobles and of Jews, tens of thousands of whom died as agents of the hated regime. Unable to win the war outright against a resurgent Poland, Khmelnytsky sought a protector, and by the Treaty of Pereyaslav (1654) he placed the Cossack Host under the tsar of Muscovy, an act whose meaning, alliance or submission, Russia and Ukraine have argued ever since. The Russo-Polish War that followed (1654-1667) devastated Ukraine, and the Truce of Andrusovo divided it: the left bank of the Dnieper and Kiev to Russia, the right bank to Poland.
para3: In the left-bank territories the Hetmanate survived as an autonomous state under its elected hetmans, with its own regiments, chancellery, courts and foreign relations, within the tsar's growing empire. Its golden age came under Ivan Mazepa (1687-1709): Cossack baroque churches and schools flourished, the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy made Kiev an intellectual center, and the hetman governed as a prince. But Peter the Great's demands in the Great Northern War, Cossack lives spent in northern campaigns, tsarist interference in elections, pushed Mazepa to defect to Charles XII of Sweden in 1708. Poltava destroyed them both: Mazepa died in exile, and Peter's reprisals razed the Zaporozhian Sich and tightened the screws.
para4: After Mazepa, autonomy was dismantled in stages: Peter imposed a Russian 'Little Russian Collegium', Catherine II abolished the hetmanate entirely in 1764 and the Sich itself in 1775, and serfdom was extended over the formerly free Cossack lands. The Hetmanate's regimental territories became the guberniyas of the Russian Empire. Yet the Hetmanate left a durable legacy: the office, the regiments and the Cossack myth became central to Ukrainian national identity, and the memory of Pereyaslav and Mazepa, partnership or treachery, submission or sovereignty, still frames the way Ukraine and Russia tell their shared history.

title: Enlightened Absolutism
titleline: Enlightened Absolutism - The History Web
para1: The Enlightenment was the eighteenth-century movement of reason that challenged the intellectual foundations of the old European order, and enlightened absolutism was the monarchs' attempt to use its tools without its conclusions. Its origins lay in the scientific revolution of the seventeenth century, Newton's ordered universe, and in the empiricism of Locke: if nature ran by discoverable laws and knowledge came from experience, then society, government, religion and law could be questioned and improved by reason rather than inherited by tradition. France was its heartland: Voltaire's campaigns against religious fanaticism and legal torture, Montesquieu's analysis of the separation of powers (1748), and the great Encyclopedie of Diderot and d'Alembert (1751-1772) spread critical thought through the reading public of salons, coffeehouses and clandestine print.
para2: The philosophes attacked privilege, superstition and censorship, though few were democrats or atheists. Rousseau went furthest, arguing in The Social Contract (1762) that legitimate government rested on the general will, and his celebration of natural virtue made him the prophet of both romanticism and revolution. Beyond France, the movement took national colors: Hume and Adam Smith in Scotland, whose Wealth of Nations (1776) founded economics; Beccaria's On Crimes and Punishments (1764), which reformed European penal law; Kant in Prussia defining enlightenment as the courage to think for oneself. Everywhere the new public sphere of journals, academies, masonic lodges and lending libraries created opinion as a political force.
para3: The absolute monarchs of Europe could not ignore the new ideas, and several adopted them, on their own terms. Frederick II of Prussia, flute-playing correspondent of Voltaire, abolished torture, decreed religious toleration, codified Prussian law and called himself the first servant of the state, while strengthening the army and the Junker monarchy. Catherine II of Russia corresponded with Diderot, drew on Montesquieu and Beccaria for her Nakaz (1767), bought libraries and founded schools, while extending serfdom to its widest reach and crushing Pugachev's revolt. Joseph II of Austria went furthest: thousands of decrees abolishing serfdom, dissolving monasteries, imposing toleration (1781) and Germanizing administration, a 'revolution from above' that provoked such resistance that his brother Leopold II had to undo much of it. Spain under Charles III, Portugal under Pombal, and Tuscany under Leopold also enacted 'enlightened' reforms.
para4: The partnership of reason and power had its limits, and they were soon exposed. Enlightened absolutism accepted the ends of efficiency and toleration but never the means of self-government; when the American colonies applied Locke against the king (1776) and France applied Rousseau against the Bastille (1789), the monarchs abandoned the philosophes and embraced reaction. Yet the Enlightenment had changed the terms of European politics permanently: reason of state now had to speak the language of utility, rights and public opinion, and the age's reforms, legal codes, religious toleration, secular education, the critique of torture, survived the revolutions they helped to cause.

title: The Papal States in the Age of Revolutions
titleline: The Papal States in the Age of Revolutions - The History Web
para1: The Papal States entered the modern era as one of Europe's oldest political bodies, territories across central Italy ruled by the popes as temporal sovereigns since the eighth century. The wars of the French Revolution shattered their world: French armies occupied Rome twice, carried off Pope Pius VI as a prisoner in 1798, and annexed the Papal States outright in 1809, imprisoning Pius VII after he excommunicated Napoleon. The Congress of Vienna (1815) restored the pope's lands almost intact, and for the next half century the papal government, administered by clerics, guarding against secret societies, railways and modern political ideas alike, became the byword of conservative reaction in Europe.
para2: Italian unification destroyed the temporal power piece by piece. The revolutions of 1848 drove Pius IX from Rome; the Roman Republic of Mazzini and Garibaldi ruled until French troops restored him in 1849. In 1860 the armies of Piedmont-Sardinia annexed the Romagna, the Marches and Umbria, leaving the pope only Rome and its countryside, defended by French bayonets and Catholic volunteers. When France withdrew its garrison during the Franco-Prussian War, Italian troops breached the Porta Pia on 20 September 1870 and took Rome, which became Italy's capital. Pius IX refused the Italian government's Law of Guarantees, declared himself 'prisoner of the Vatican', and forbade Catholics, under the non expedit, from taking part in Italian political life.
para3: The 'Roman Question' festered for decade after decade. Successive popes never set foot outside the Vatican walls, the non expedit kept faithful Italians out of national politics, and every Italian government maintained the unanswered Law of Guarantees. The First World War, fought between Catholic Austria and Italy, sharpened the isolation: Benedict XV's peace note of 1917 was ignored by the belligerents, and the new pope Pius XI, elected in 1922, set about rebuilding the Church's missions - and looking for a way to end the quarrel with Italy.
para4: By 1924 the standoff had lasted fifty-four years: the pope sovereign over a palace and a garden, Italy's capital seated in the city the popes still claimed, and no settlement in sight - though discreet contacts had begun. The Roman Question had shaped two generations of Catholic politics, from the culture wars of Bismarck's Germany to the anticlerical laws of republican France, and it remained, as it had been since 1870, the open wound of the Italian state.

title: The Balkan Wars
titleline: The Balkan Wars - The History Web
para1: The Balkan Wars of 1912-1913 destroyed Ottoman power in Europe and set the stage for the First World War. Behind them lay the slow Ottoman retreat from the Balkans and the ambitions of the new Christian states, Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece and Montenegro, whose peoples still lived under Ottoman rule in Macedonia, Albania and Thrace. In 1912, encouraged by Russian diplomacy and by Italy's war with the Ottomans in Libya, the four states formed the Balkan League, and in October 1912 they attacked together. The First Balkan War was a rout: the Serbs took Kosovo and Macedonia, the Greeks took Thessaloniki, just ahead of the Bulgarians, and the Bulgarians drove to within miles of Constantinople, while the great powers recognized an independent Albania to keep Serbia off the Adriatic.
para2: The victors immediately fell out over the spoils. Bulgaria, which had done the heaviest fighting, claimed most of Macedonia; Serbia, shut out of Albania, demanded compensation there; Greece and Romania also held claims against Sofia. When negotiations failed, Bulgaria attacked its former allies on 29 June 1913, opening the Second Balkan War. Serbia, Greece, Montenegro and Romania, which seized southern Dobruja, all counterattacked, and the Ottoman Empire returned to recover Adrianople (Edirne). Within a month Bulgaria was crushed and forced to sign the Treaty of Bucharest (August 1913), losing territory on every side.
para3: The wars doubled the size of Serbia, Greece, Montenegro and Romania, cut the Ottoman Empire back to a corner of Thrace, and confirmed Albanian independence. But they left three poisonous legacies. First, a humiliated Bulgaria nursed revenge, joining the Central Powers in 1915 to recover what it had lost. Second, a triumphant Serbia, now twice its size, terrified Austria-Hungary, which saw South Slav nationalism, armed by Belgrade, reaching into its own provinces; the Sarajevo assassination of June 1914 grew directly from the wars' settlement. Third, the wars introduced mass ethnic violence into southeastern Europe: villages burned, populations expelled, atrocities documented by an international commission of 1914 that read like a preview of the century to come.
para4: The Balkan Wars also revealed the great powers' near-paralysis: Austria-Hungary mobilized, Russia backed Serbia, and the Concert of Europe, through the London Conference of ambassadors, managed only to draw Albania's borders while the fighting decided everything else. When the next Balkan crisis came in July 1914, no one believed diplomacy would contain it, and the alliance system that had kept the peace for forty years pulled Europe into a general war in a matter of weeks.

title: Russia from Decembrists to 1905
titleline: Russia from Decembrists to 1905 - The History Web
para1: The Revolution of 1905 was Russia's first great revolutionary crisis, the 'dress rehearsal', as Lenin called it, for 1917. Its causes lay in the contradictions of the tsarist autocracy: a rapidly industrializing economy and an oppressed working class living in squalor, land-hungry peasants, restive national minorities on the empire's edges, and an intelligentsia excluded from political life, all ruled by Nicholas II, a weak tsar committed to unlimited autocracy. Defeat in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905) exposed the regime's incompetence to the world, and on 22 January 1905 the crisis broke: troops fired on a peaceful procession of St Petersburg workers marching with icons and petitions to the Winter Palace, led by the priest Father Gapon. 'Bloody Sunday' killed hundreds and destroyed the myth of the benevolent tsar.
para2: The empire erupted. Strikes spread from city to city, a general strike in October paralyzed the railways; peasants burned manor houses; mutinies shook the armed forces, most famously on the battleship Potemkin in Odessa in June; soviets, workers' councils, appeared for the first time, the St Petersburg Soviet led briefly by the young Leon Trotsky; and from Poland to the Caucasus the non-Russian peoples rose. Every strand of opposition, liberal zemstvo men demanding a constitution, Socialist Revolutionaries among the peasants, Marxist Social Democrats, national movements, surged at once against the autocracy.
para3: Faced with the general strike and a still-unreliable army, Nicholas II conceded: the October Manifesto (30 October 1905) promised civil liberties and an elected parliament, the State Duma, with legislative powers. The concession split the opposition: liberals accepted and went home, workers and socialists fought on, and in December the Moscow Soviet's armed uprising was crushed by artillery in the streets of Presnya. With the army loyal and the regime's enemies divided, the government regained control through 1906, backed by pogroms against Jews and revolutionaries, field courts-martial and mass arrests, the 'Stolypin necktie' of the gallows.
para4: The Fundamental Laws of April 1906 then hollowed out the promised constitution: the tsar kept control of the army, foreign policy and ministers, and could dismiss the Duma at will. Four Dumas were elected on ever-narrower franchises, and Stolypin's agrarian reforms tried to build a class of loyal peasant proprietors while thousands of revolutionaries went to Siberia or exile. The 1905 revolution failed, but it had shown that the autocracy could be shaken: the soviet was invented, the parties were battle-tested, and the workers and soldiers who made 1905 would make February and October 1917.

title: The Eighty Years' War
titleline: The Eighty Years' War - The History Web
para1: The Eighty Years' War (1568-1648), also called the Dutch Revolt, created the Dutch Republic out of rebellion against the Spanish Habsburgs. The Seventeen Provinces of the Netherlands, among Europe's richest and most urbanized lands, were inherited by Philip II of Spain, whose government attacked the privileges of the provinces' estates, quartered Spanish garrisons, planned new bishoprics, and sent the Inquisition against spreading Protestantism. Resistance hardened after 1566, when the nobles' petition of the Compromise was dismissed, the petitioners proudly adopting the slur 'Beggars', and Calvinist mobs in the 'Iconoclastic Fury' smashed church images across the provinces. Philip answered with the Duke of Alba's Army of Flanders and the Council of Troubles, which executed the counts Egmont and Hornes in Brussels in 1568 and drove thousands into exile.
para2: William of Orange, the Silent, organized the revolt from exile, and in 1572 the Sea Beggars seized Brielle, triggering general insurrection in Holland and Zeeland. Alba's terror, the sack of Mechelen, Zutphen and Naarden, the siege and massacre of Haarlem and the relief of Leiden, whose dikes were cut to drown the siege, failed to break the northern provinces, united behind William in 1576's Pacification of Ghent after the Spanish Fury at Antwerp horrified the whole Netherlands. But Parma's reconquest of the Catholic south in the 1580s, taking Antwerp in 1585 after a brilliant siege, split the provinces permanently: the south remained Spanish, the future Belgium; the seven northern provinces had formed the Union of Utrecht (1579) and in 1581, by the Act of Abjuration, formally deposed Philip, Europe's first modern declaration of independence.
para3: After William's assassination in 1584, the young republic survived through trade wealth, sea power and the military reforms of Maurice of Nassau, who with Oldenbarnevelt built a professional army that retook Breda and the eastern fortresses. England's war with Spain, ending in the Armada's defeat (1588), relieved the pressure, and the Dutch took the war to the sea and the world: the East India Company (1602) and West India Company (1621) seized Portuguese and Spanish possessions from Brazil to Indonesia. A Twelve Years' Truce (1609) acknowledged facts without recognition, but war resumed with the Thirty Years' War, whose Dutch theater saw Frederick Henry's sieges, the Battle of the Downs (1639) destroying Spanish sea power, and the Franco-Dutch alliance against Spain.
para4: The Peace of Munster, part of Westphalia (30 January 1648), ended the war: Spain finally recognized the independence of the Republic of the Seven United Netherlands, keeping the Scheldt closed to strangle Antwerp for Amsterdam's benefit. The war had created Europe's most unusual state: a merchant republic without a king, tolerant by the standards of the age, the financial and naval center of the world, whose Golden Age of Rembrandt, Vermeer and Spinoza was built while the fighting continued. The southern Netherlands stayed under Spanish, then Austrian, rule until 1794.

title: The Great Northern War
titleline: The Great Northern War - The History Web
para1: The Great Northern War (1700-1721) decided whether Sweden or Russia would dominate northeastern Europe. Sweden's Baltic empire, stretching from Bremen to Narva, had humbled its neighbors, and in 1697 the fifteen-year-old Charles XII inherited it. Three of them, Denmark, Augustus the Strong's Saxony-Poland, and Peter the Great's Russia, allied to dismember the empire while the boy-king reigned. Charles answered with a speed that stunned Europe: he landed near Copenhagen and knocked Denmark out of the war in August 1700, then shipped to Estonia and in a November blizzard annihilated a Russian army four times his size at Narva, capturing its guns and its generals. Peter's new model army had been destroyed in an afternoon.
para2: Instead of marching on Moscow, Charles turned west to deal with Augustus, whose Saxon and Polish territories he spent six years conquering. By the Treaty of Altranstadt (1706) he deposed Augustus from the Polish throne and imposed his own candidate, Stanislaus Leszczynski. The delay proved fatal. Peter rebuilt his army on the Swedish model, took Narva and Dorpat, founded St Petersburg on conquered Ingrian soil (1703), and drew Charles into a war of attrition. When Charles finally invaded Russia in 1708, allied with the Cossack hetman Mazepa, Peter denied him supplies, winter and Russian scorched-earth columns bled the march, and at Poltava on 8 July 1709 Peter destroyed the Swedish army outright. Charles fled into Ottoman exile at Bender, where he spent five years trying to draw the sultan into the war.
para3: While Charles was away, the empire he had defended fell apart. Augustus returned to Poland; Denmark re-entered the war; Hanover, Prussia and Russia took the Swedish possessions in Germany and the Baltic; and Peter's new fleet defeated the Swedes at Gangut (1714). Charles returned to a ruined kingdom in 1715, defended Stralsund, and was killed by a shot through the head besieging Fredriksten in Norway in 1718. His sister Ulrika Eleonora and then her husband Frederick I made peace piecemeal: the Treaties of Stockholm (1719-1720) ceded Bremen-Verden to Hanover and part of Pomerania to Prussia, and the Treaty of Nystad (1721) ceded Livonia, Estonia, Ingria and eastern Karelia to Russia.
para4: Nystad ended Sweden's age as a great power and confirmed Russia's arrival as one: Peter proclaimed himself emperor the same year, and St Petersburg became the new capital of a Russia that now dominated the Baltic and, increasingly, the politics of Poland, Germany and Scandinavia. The war also transformed both losers and winners: Sweden turned from absolutism to its parliamentary Age of Liberty, while Russia's victory rested on the forced Westernization, conscription, industry and a fleet built from nothing, that would define the empire for two centuries.

title: The Greek War of Independence
titleline: The Greek War of Independence - The History Web
para1: The Greek War of Independence (1821-1832) freed the first nation of the Ottoman Empire's European provinces and made Greece an independent kingdom. Its background was the national revival of the eighteenth century: the Greeks of the diaspora, of the Phanariot administration and of the merchant fleets, the ideas of the French Revolution, and the secret society Filiki Eteria, founded in Odessa in 1814, which organized the rising. In March 1821 Alexander Ypsilantis crossed into the Danubian Principalities hoping for Russian support, and was crushed; but in the Peloponnese the revolt proclaimed on 25 March spread like fire. By autumn the rebels held most of the peninsula: Tripolitsa fell in October 1821, amid massacres of its Muslim inhabitants that were answered by Ottoman reprisals, above all the execution of the Patriarch Gregory V in Constantinople and the massacres of Chios (1822), where tens of thousands were killed or enslaved.
para2: The revolution nearly destroyed itself through civil war: rival governments, military chiefs and regional factions fought two civil wars in 1823-1825 even as they fought the sultan. Mahmud II called in his powerful vassal Muhammad Ali of Egypt, whose son Ibrahim Pasha landed with a modern army in 1825 and reconquered the Peloponnese systematically; Missolonghi, defended for a year, fell in April 1826, its garrison dying in a famous sortie that Byron's death there in 1824 had already made a European symbol. Athens fell in 1827, and the revolution survived only in a few pockets. Greece was saved by the powers: Britain, France and Russia, their publics ablaze with philhellenism, their cabinets pursuing advantage, mediated, and when negotiations failed their combined fleet destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at Navarino (October 1827), the last great battle of the age of sail.
para3: Russia's declaration of war (1828) and its victories on the Danube forced the sultan to terms. The Treaty of Adrianople (1829) gave Greece autonomy, and the London Protocol (1830), following the assassination of the first governor, the capable Ioannis Kapodistrias, made Greece an independent kingdom under the powers' guarantee. In 1832 the seventeen-year-old Bavarian prince Otto arrived as king with a Bavarian administration; his autocratic rule provoked a constitution in 1843, and the kingdom's borders, which excluded most Greeks, in Thessaly, Epirus, Macedonia, Crete and the islands, drove a century of irredentism under the 'Megali Idea'.
para4: The Greek revolution's significance reached far beyond the Aegean. It was the first successful national revolution in Ottoman Europe, the model and the precedent for the Serbs, Romanians and Bulgarians who followed; it demonstrated that the Concert of Europe would not always defend the territorial status quo against national revolt; and the philhellenic movement, volunteers, loans, poems, made nationalism a European cause. Modern Greece, though small and repeatedly rescued, had shown that the empires of the old order could be broken.

title: The Russo-Turkish Wars
titleline: The Russo-Turkish Wars - The History Web
para1: The Russo-Turkish Wars were the long series of conflicts, twelve major wars between 1568 and 1917, through which Russia expanded southward at the Ottoman Empire's expense. The early clashes were frontier wars over the steppe: Astrakhan, the Azov fortress, and the Crimean Khanate, the Ottomans' vassal, whose slave-raiding horsemen burned Moscow itself in 1571. Peter the Great took Azov (1696), lost it again on the Pruth (1711), and the eighteenth century turned the wars into a systematic Russian advance: by the Treaty of Kucuk Kaynarca (1774), after Catherine the Great's armies won at Kagul, Russia gained a foothold on the Black Sea, the right to navigate it, and a claimed protectorate over Ottoman Orthodox Christians. Nine years later Catherine annexed Crimea outright.
para2: The nineteenth century made the wars the core of the 'Eastern Question'. Russia presented itself as the protector of the sultan's Orthodox subjects, Greeks, Serbs, Romanians, Bulgarians, while Britain and France feared the Straits falling into Russian hands and repeatedly propped the Ottoman Empire up. The wars of 1806-1812 and 1828-1829 gave Russia Bessarabia and the Danube's mouth and helped free Greece; the war of 1853-1856, the Crimean War, was Russia's great reversal, when Britain, France and Sardinia intervened to save the sultan and neutralized the Black Sea. Russia answered with expansion in the Caucasus and Central Asia, and with pan-Slav support for the Balkan Christians.
para3: The great war came in 1877. After the Ottomans crushed Bulgarian and Serbian risings with massacres that outraged Europe, Alexander II declared war. Russian armies crossed the Danube, were held for months at Plevna by Osman Pasha's heroic defense, then broke through the Balkan mountains in winter to within reach of Constantinople. The Treaty of San Stefano (March 1878) created a huge autonomous Bulgaria and recognized the independence of Serbia, Montenegro and Romania; but the powers refused a Russian-made Balkans, and the Congress of Berlin, Bismarck as 'honest broker', cut Bulgaria in three, returned Macedonia to the sultan, gave Bosnia to Austria-Hungary's administration, and Cyprus to Britain. Russia had won the war and lost much of the peace.
para4: The wars' legacy was the modern Balkans and Russia's Black Sea position: Romania, Serbia, Montenegro and Bulgaria owed their independence substantially to Russian arms, while the Caucasus, Armenia's eastern lands and the fortress of Kars passed to the tsars. The two empires fought once more in the First World War, the disasters of Sarikamish and the Russian occupation of Erzurum and Trebizond, before both collapsed into revolution in 1917. The new Turkey that emerged from its own war of independence settled the last accounts with Russia's successor at the Straits and the Caucasus frontier, closing a rivalry that had lasted two and a half centuries.

title: The Concert of Europe
titleline: The Concert of Europe - The History Web
para1: The Concert of Europe was the informal system of great-power consultation that managed European affairs for a century, from the Congress of Vienna in 1815 to the First World War. It had no charter, no headquarters and no rules; it rested on two ideas: that the five great powers, Britain, Austria, Russia, Prussia and, from 1818, France, shared a common interest in preventing any one of them from dominating the continent, and that general war could be avoided if the powers met to settle dangerous questions together before fighting over them. The Vienna settlement itself, partitioning Europe by dynastic legitimacy and balance of power, was its founding act, and the Quadruple Alliance's congresses were meant to be its instrument.
para2: The early Concert worked through congress diplomacy: Aix-la-Chapelle (1818) admitted France to the club; Troppau, Laibach and Verona (1820-1822) quarreled over Austria's suppression of the Italian revolutions, driving Britain toward separation. The system bent but held through its first crises: Greek independence was managed jointly in 1827-1832 against the principle of legitimacy; Belgium's secession from the Netherlands (1830-1839) was negotiated into guaranteed neutrality; the Eastern crises of 1840 and 1878 were settled at London and Berlin without general war. Even the Crimean War (1853-1856), the Concert's worst failure, ended in a congress at Paris that readmitted the Ottoman Empire to the system.
para3: The mid-century wars of unification tested the Concert and, surprisingly, left its habit intact: Prussia's wars of 1864-1871 redrew the map without a general coalition forming against it, and Bismarck, having unified Germany, became the Concert's chief manager, his alliance system, the Congress of Berlin (1878), and the Mediterranean agreements all designed to localize conflicts and keep France isolated. After Bismarck's fall in 1890 the system's threads loosened: alliances hardened into the Triple Alliance and the Franco-Russian, then Anglo-French, blocs, imperial rivalries moved competition to Africa and Asia, and the arms race and war plans made mobilization schedules stronger than diplomacy.
para4: The Concert still scored late successes, the Algeciras Conference (1906) on Morocco, the London Conference (1912-1913) that drew Albania's borders after the Balkan Wars, but each success came at the price of entrenching the two armed camps. When the July Crisis of 1914 began, Austria-Hungary deliberately avoided the conference method that had defused earlier crises, Germany backed its ultimatums, Russia mobilized, and the alliance machinery the Concert had failed to replace pulled Europe into general war. The League of Nations, born in 1920, was in its way an attempt to give the Concert's idea, peace through consultation among powers, the permanent institutions it had always lacked.

title: The German Confederation
titleline: The German Confederation - The History Web
para1: Germany before unification was not a country but a civilization of states. The Holy Roman Empire had dissolved into, after 1648, some three hundred effectively sovereign principalities, duchies, bishoprics, free cities and knights' estates, the Kleinstaaterei that made Germany a patchwork of tolls, laws, armies and courts. The Empire provided a loose constitutional frame, the emperor, the Imperial Diet at Regensburg, imperial courts, but real power lay with the princes, above all the Habsburg emperors in Vienna and the Hohenzollern kings of Prussia, whose dualism dominated German history from 1740.
para2: Napoleon simplified the map by conquest. The mediatization of 1803 abolished most of the ecclesiastical states and folded the small territories into larger ones; the old Empire itself was dissolved in 1806, when a league of German princes formed the Confederation of the Rhine under French protection. The reforms of the era, Prussia's Stein and Hardenberg measures after the catastrophe of Jena (1806), Bavaria's and Baden's modernizations, created efficient centralized administrations, emancipated peasants and Jews to varying degrees, and, in the Wars of Liberation (1813-1815), awakened a German national consciousness that the restored princes refused to satisfy.
para3: The Congress of Vienna replaced the Empire with the German Confederation (Deutscher Bund), thirty-nine states under Austrian presidency with a diet at Frankfurt, deliberately too weak to act except in suppressing nationalism, Metternich's Carlsbad Decrees (1819) made that explicit. Economic integration outran politics: Prussia's Zollverein (customs union, 1834) bound most German states into a free-trade area that pointedly excluded Austria, making Prussia the economic leader of Germany a generation before it became the political one. The liberal and national movement of the Vormarz era, Burschenschaften and the Frankfurt Parliament of 1848, demanded unity and constitutions and was defeated, leaving unity to be achieved by state power instead.
para4: The path to unification ran through the rivalry of the two German great powers. Prussia under King William I and, from 1862, Bismarck built the army that would decide the German question, first taking Schleswig and Holstein from Denmark with Austria in 1864, then provoking the Austro-Prussian War of 1866: Koniggratz expelled Austria from German affairs, dissolved the Confederation, and let Prussia annex Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau and Frankfurt outright, founding the North German Confederation. The southern states were drawn in through the Franco-Prussian War (1870-1871), and on 18 January 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. The centuries of particularism ended in a federal empire dominated by Prussia.

title: The Deluge and the Swedish-Polish Wars
titleline: The Deluge and the Swedish-Polish Wars - The History Web
para1: The Polish-Swedish Wars were a long series of conflicts between the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and Sweden, fought above all for control of the Baltic coast between 1563 and 1721. Their roots were both commercial, the customs wealth of Riga and the Vistula grain trade, and dynastic: Sigismund III Vasa, elected king of Poland in 1587, was also the hereditary heir of Sweden, and when his uncle seized the Swedish throne as Charles IX in 1600 and deposed him, Sigismund refused to renounce his claim. The resulting wars began in Livonia, where Swedish and Commonwealth armies fought over Estonia and Latvia through the 1620s: Gustavus Adolphus took Riga (1621) and most of Livonia, and from 1626 carried the war into Royal Prussia, where the Poles under Stanislaw Koniecpolski held him in check for three years.
para2: The truces that punctuated the fighting masked Sweden's gradual gain: by the Altmark Truce (1629) Sweden kept Livonia and the right to toll the Vistula ports, financing the army that Gustavus then led into Germany. The Commonwealth's eastern wars, against Cossacks, Russia and the Ottomans, gave Sweden its great opportunity. In 1655, while Poland reeled from the Khmelnytsky Uprising and the Russian invasion, Charles X Gustav attacked, and the Commonwealth nearly died: in the 'Deluge', the Swedish army overran and occupied most of the country by October 1655, and King John Casimir fled abroad. The occupation collapsed as Polish peasants and gentry rose against Swedish control, the defense of the Jasna Gora monastery at Czestochowa became the national legend, and by 1660 the Peace of Oliva ended the Deluge with Poland's sovereignty intact but exhausted.
para3: The last round came in the Great Northern War, when Augustus II the Strong, elector of Saxony and king of Poland, joined Russia and Denmark against Charles XII. The war devastated the Commonwealth: Charles deposed Augustus, imposed Stanislaus Leszczynski (1704), and used Poland as his base for the Russian campaign that ended at Poltava (1709). Augustus returned, but the Commonwealth had become a theater for other powers' armies and a protectorate of Russia, which guaranteed its 'Golden Liberty' constitution precisely because that constitution made the state ungovernable.
para4: The long wars with Sweden cost the Commonwealth its Baltic provinces, its best trade ports and, ultimately, its position as a great power: by 1721 Poland was financially broken, its army tiny, its liberum veto paralyzing reform, while Sweden too had spent its empire in the struggle. Both Baltic powers were eclipsed by Russia and Prussia, and when Poland was partitioned by its neighbors (1772-1795), Swedish interference was among the fatal weaknesses the partitioners exploited.

title: The Tudor Conquest of Ireland
titleline: The Tudor Conquest of Ireland - The History Web
para1: The Tudor Conquest of Ireland. Henry VIII began it with a legal revolution: in 1541 the Irish Parliament declared him King of Ireland, ending the medieval lordship and proclaiming that the whole island - Gaelic chiefs and old English lords alike - now owed obedience to one crown. The policy that followed, called surrender and regrant, asked the chiefs to give up their lands and titles and receive them back from the king as English earls and barons, holding by English law. For a while it worked: O'Neill became Earl of Tyrone, O'Brien Earl of Thomond, and the great houses of Gaelic Ireland took their seats in the Dublin parliament.
para2: Beneath the conciliation ran a harder current. Where submission failed, the Tudors planted: loyal English settlers were planted on confiscated lands, beginning in Laois and Offaly in the 1550s, renamed King's County and Queen's County. Under Elizabeth the pace quickened. The long Desmond rebellion in Munster (1569-1583) ended in famine and mass confiscation, and the rebels' lands were granted to English undertakers - the Munster Plantation, whose settlers included the poet Edmund Spenser and the adventurer Walter Raleigh. Garrisons, martial law and the composition of Connacht pressed English government into every province.
para3: The Gaelic world made its last stand in Ulster. Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, and Hugh Roe O'Donnell raised the north in the Nine Years' War (1594-1603), destroyed an English army at the Yellow Ford, and brought a Spanish landing at Kinsale. Defeat there broke the rebellion, and though Tyrone submitted on terms, the old order was finished. England had at last conquered all of Ireland - at staggering cost in money and Irish lives.
para4: The conquest was completed by law and settlement. English common law replaced the brehon law, the shiring of the whole island tied every acre to the crown's courts, and when Tyrone and the northern earls fled to the continent in 1607, their lands were confiscated for the Plantation of Ulster, the largest of all. The Tudor century in Ireland set the mold of everything after: confiscation, plantation, and a conquered land ruled from Dublin Castle for the English crown.

title: The Nine Years' War in Ireland
titleline: The Nine Years' War in Ireland - The History Web
para1: The Nine Years' War. Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, was England's man in Ulster - raised partly at the English court, enriched by the crown, and counted the most loyal of Gaelic lords - until the advancing English administration cornered him. In 1594, pushed past endurance by the sheriffs and garrisons closing on his lordship, he went into rebellion with his ally Hugh Roe O'Donnell of Tyrconnell, and the war that followed came nearer than any other to driving Tudor England out of Ireland.
para2: O'Neill fought a new kind of Irish war. He trained his kern and gallowglass in continental fashion, armed them with muskets bought with Spanish gold, and refused the pitched battles the English wanted, fighting instead from ambush, bog and wood. On 14 August 1598 he caught the Marshal of England, Sir Henry Bagenal, marching to relieve the Blackwater fort, and at the Yellow Ford destroyed the finest army Elizabeth had in Ireland - some two thousand men killed or captured. All Ireland rose; Munster's plantations were overrun in days, and a royal clerk wrote home that the kingdom was all but lost.
para3: Elizabeth sent her favorite, the Earl of Essex, with the largest army of the reign - seventeen thousand men - and he accomplished nothing, wasted his army in the south, and met O'Neill only in a private parley that ruined him at court. His successor, Mountjoy, was made of sterner stuff: he ground Ulster down with garrisons, burned crops, and famine. The war became an endurance contest O'Neill could not win.
para4: The end came at Kinsale. A Spanish expedition landed there in September 1601, and O'Neill and O'Donnell marched the length of Ireland in winter to join it. Mountjoy besieged the town, and on 24 December 1601 the Irish attacked to break the siege and were routed in an hour. O'Donnell fled to Spain and died there; O'Neill held out until March 1603, submitting days after Elizabeth herself had died. The war had cost England nearly two million pounds and Ireland perhaps a hundred thousand dead, and it left the Gaelic order broken beyond repair - the gateway to the Flight of the Earls and the Plantation of Ulster.

title: The Flight of the Earls and the Plantation of Ulster
titleline: The Flight of the Earls and the Plantation of Ulster - The History Web
para1: The Flight of the Earls. On 14 September 1607 a French ship slipped out of Rathmullan on Lough Swilly carrying ninety-nine passengers: Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, Rory O'Donnell, Earl of Tyrconnell, their families and followers - the last great lords of Gaelic Ulster. Beaten in war, watched by Dublin Castle, and fearing arrest for conspiracies real or invented, they sailed for Spain and ended in Rome, where Tyrone died in 1616. They meant, most believed, to return with foreign help. They never came back, and Gaelic Ireland's old leadership went with them.
para2: Into the vacuum came the Plantation of Ulster. The flight was judged treason, and six counties - Armagh, Cavan, Donegal, Fermanagh, Tyrone and Coleraine, some half a million acres - were declared forfeit to the crown. The lands were measured out to undertakers, English and Scottish landlords bound to settle British tenants, build bawns and castles, and keep no Irish on the best land. The City of London's guilds took Coleraine, rebuilt Derry within walls that still stand, and gave it their name: Londonderry.
para3: The plan drew a new map of peoples. Tens of thousands of lowland Scots and northern English crossed to Ulster in the following decades - farmers, weavers, smiths - settling beside a dispossessed Irish population that remained on the poorer lands as laborers and tenants. English, Scots and Irish, Protestant and Catholic, were planted cheek by jowl in the most deliberately engineered colonization of the British Isles, and the province's divided character ever since was laid down in those decades.
para4: The dispossessed did not forget. In October 1641 the Irish of Ulster rose under Sir Phelim O'Neill to seize back what had been taken, and the rising - with its massacres of settlers, grotesquely magnified in the telling - ignited a decade of war and a new cycle of confiscation under Cromwell and the Restoration. The Flight of the Earls had been meant to end the Irish question in the north; it made Ulster instead the hardest knot in the islands' history, still being untied four centuries later.

title: Confederate Ireland and the Cromwellian Conquest
titleline: Confederate Ireland and the Cromwellian Conquest - The History Web
para1: Confederate Ireland. In October 1641, with King and Parliament sliding toward war in England, the Catholic Irish of Ulster rose to seize back the planted lands, and the rising spread across the island. Out of it the Catholic landowners - Gaelic Irish and Old English alike - built something Ireland had never had: a government of their own. The Catholic Confederation, founded at Kilkenny in 1642, ran an assembly, courts, taxes, a mint and armies, and for seven years ruled most of Ireland in the name of King Charles, while negotiating to save both his crown and their religion.
para2: The Confederates were divided from the start. The Old English wanted a deal with the king on any workable terms; the Gaelic Irish, and the papal nuncio Rinuccini, demanded full restoration of the Catholic Church and the confiscated lands. Their armies won the war's one great Irish victory - Owen Roe O'Neill's destruction of a Scottish army at Benburb in 1646 - and threw the advantage away in quarrels. Ormond's royalist peace split the Confederation, and its divided armies were beaten one by one.
para3: In August 1649 Oliver Cromwell landed at Dublin with the New Model Army, and what followed has never been forgotten. In September he stormed Drogheda and put the garrison - some two and a half thousand men - to the sword, with many civilians dying in the slaughter; in October Wexford suffered the same fate. The other garrisons did not wait: town after town surrendered rather than face him. Within nine months Cromwell had broken organized resistance in the east and south and sailed home, leaving his generals to finish a conquest completed, amid famine and plague, by 1653.
para4: The settlement was as hard as the conquest. The Act of Settlement of 1652 confiscated the lands of the Catholic landowning class wholesale; its owners were transplanted to Connacht - to hell or Connaught ran the phrase - or shipped to the colonies, and their acres went to soldiers and adventurers. By 1660 the Catholic share of Irish land had fallen from about sixty per cent to barely twenty. Cromwell spent less than a year in Ireland, and his name has been a curse-word there for nearly four centuries.

title: The Williamite War and the Battle of the Boyne
titleline: The Williamite War and the Battle of the Boyne - The History Web
para1: The Williamite War. When the Catholic James II lost his English throne in the Glorious Revolution of 1688, he looked to Ireland to win it back. Ireland's Catholics, ruled by the Protestant minority and longing to undo the Cromwellian land settlement, rallied to him; its Protestants, above all in Ulster, shut the gates of Derry and held out for William of Orange. In March 1689 James landed at Kinsale with French money and officers, and Ireland became the battlefield of two kings - and of Europe, for Louis XIV of France backed James to keep William's England out of the continental war.
para2: The siege of Derry made the war's legend: for a hundred and five days in 1689 the apprentice boys who had shut the gates and the citizens behind the walls held out through starvation until the relief ship Mountjoy broke the boom across the Foyle. Meanwhile James's Patriot Parliament in Dublin attainted the Protestant landholders wholesale. The decision came the following summer, when William himself landed with a great international army - Dutch, Danish, Huguenot, English and Ulster Protestant.
para3: On 1 July 1690 (11 July by the modern calendar) the two armies met at the River Boyne, west of Drogheda. William forced the crossings at Oldbridge while his cavalry worked around the Irish flank; James's army, outflanked and outnumbered, retreated in good order, and James himself rode for Dublin, then France, earning among his own people the name Seamus an Chaca - James the... flighty. The Boyne was not a great battle by numbers - perhaps two thousand dead - but it decided the war and the century, and it is still commemorated every twelfth of July.
para4: The war went on another year: William was bloodily repulsed at Limerick in 1690, the Jacobite army was broken at Aughrim in 1691 - the bloodiest battle ever fought in Ireland - and the war ended with the Treaty of Limerick, whose promised toleration the victors promptly set aside. The Protestant Ascendancy was secured for a century, the penal laws followed, and another generation of Irish soldiers - the Wild Geese - sailed away to fight in the armies of France and Spain.

title: The Penal Laws and the Protestant Ascendancy
titleline: The Penal Laws and the Protestant Ascendancy - The History Web
para1: The Penal Laws. After the Williamite victory, the Protestant minority that owned Ireland legislated to make sure it could never be challenged. Between 1695 and 1728 the Irish parliament - from which Catholics were excluded - passed the body of statutes remembered as the penal laws. Catholics were barred from Parliament, the law, the army, the universities and public office; forbidden to buy land from Protestants, to inherit it whole, to carry arms, to own a horse worth more than five pounds, to teach school or to go abroad for education. Catholic worship itself was regulated and its bishops banished.
para2: The deepest cuts were economic. The law of gavelkind forced a Catholic's land to be divided among all his sons, splintering estates with every generation - unless one son conformed to the established church, in which case he took it all. The aim was not to convert the Irish, as even the Ascendancy admitted, but to impoverish and disarm them. In practice the laws were enforced unevenly: great Catholic merchants quietly grew rich in the ports, and the countryside kept its priests and its hedge schools, where a barefoot schoolmaster taught Latin and Greek behind a hedge.
para3: The eighteenth century in Protestant Ireland was the age of the Ascendancy at its ease: Dublin grew into the second city of the British Isles, graced with the Custom House, the Four Courts and the wide Georgian squares that still define it, while its parliament - Grattan's Parliament after 1782 - won a measure of legislative independence. It was an elegant prosperity resting on exclusion: the great majority of the nation were tenants without rights, and tithes for a church they did not attend were collected from Catholic cottiers at the point of distress.
para4: The system rotted from within and without. The French Revolution and the rising of 1798 terrified London into union, and the penal laws themselves were progressively repealed: the franchise in 1793, most offices over following decades, and in 1829 Daniel O'Connell's mass movement forced Catholic Emancipation through a frightened Parliament. But the memory of the penal era - the five-pound horse, the hedge school, the priest-hunter - entered the Irish national story as its century of humiliation, and powered the politics that followed.

title: The United Irishmen and the 1798 Rebellion
titleline: The United Irishmen and the 1798 Rebellion - The History Web
para1: The United Irishmen. The French Revolution found its most devoted British and Irish disciples in Belfast, of all places, where in 1791 a young Dublin lawyer named Theobald Wolfe Tone founded the Society of United Irishmen with the Presbyterian radicals of the north. Their program was revolutionary and new: to unite Catholic, Protestant and Dissenter in one Irish nation, break the connection with England, and win a republic - by French arms if necessary. In an island defined by sect, the United Irishmen proposed to abolish sect itself.
para2: The society swept the country, recruiting hundreds of thousands through oath-bound cells, its genius being to wed the politics of the French Revolution to the grievances of the Catholic countryside. Wolfe Tone went to Paris and talked the Directory into invasion; in December 1796 a French fleet carrying fifteen thousand troops reached Bantry Bay and was scattered by storms, within sight of the Irish coast. The government answered with terror: the disarming of Ulster, floggings, pitch-caps and house-burnings by the yeomanry broke the society's organization and drove it toward a premature rising.
para3: The rebellion came in May 1798, after the government had swept up the Leinster leadership. Dublin, disarmed and leaderless, did not rise; but the countryside did. In Wexford the rebels won astonishing early victories, took Enniscorthy and Wexford town, and held the county for weeks until the great army converging on Vinegar Hill broke them on 21 June. In Ulster the Presbyterian risings at Antrim and Ballynahinch were crushed in days. A small French landing under General Humbert at Killala in August beat a British army at Castlebar - the Races of Castlebar - and surrendered a fortnight later. Wolfe Tone, taken with a second French squadron, cut his own throat rather than be hanged.
para4: Perhaps thirty thousand died in a few months, rebels and loyalists and civilians, with sectarian massacre on both sides - Scullabogue and the Gibbet Rath among the stains. The rebellion's failure killed the Irish parliament: London bought the votes to abolish it, and the Act of Union followed in 1800. But the United Irishmen had founded the enduring tradition of Irish republicanism, and Tone - Protestant, revolutionary, separatist - became its founding father.

title: The Act of Union, 1801
titleline: The Act of Union, 1801 - The History Web
para1: The Act of Union. The rebellion of 1798 frightened the British government into a constitutional revolution. Ireland, ruled since 1782 by its own Protestant parliament in Dublin, had proved it could drift toward revolution and French invasion; the prime minister William Pitt resolved to absorb it. The instrument was a legislative union on the model of Scotland's in 1707: the Irish and British parliaments would merge into one Parliament of the United Kingdom at Westminster, and the two kingdoms would become, from 1 January 1801, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.
para2: The Irish parliament had to vote itself out of existence, and it would not do so for nothing. The first attempt in 1799 was defeated; the second, in 1800, was carried by the most systematic bribery in the history of either parliament: peerages, pensions, offices and hard cash - the British government spent and promised on a colossal scale, and compensated the borough-owners whose pocket seats were abolished. Catholic support was courted with a promise Pitt could not keep: that union would bring Catholic Emancipation, the right of Catholics to sit in Parliament.
para3: On the first day of 1801 the United Kingdom came into being, with a new flag - the Union Jack, joining the crosses of St George and St Andrew with the saltire of St Patrick - and a hundred Irish members at Westminster. Dublin lost its parliament, and with it much of its political class and prosperity: the great Georgian capital slowly became a backwater of a legislature three hundred miles away, a decline its unionist opponents never tired of mourning.
para4: Emancipation did not come: King George III refused it, Pitt resigned, and the broken promise poisoned the union from its birth. Daniel O'Connell built his career on undoing it, first through Emancipation in 1829, then through the Repeal movement of the 1840s. Every strand of later Irish politics - O'Connell's repeal, Parnell's Home Rule, the separatism of 1916 - defined itself against the union of 1801, until the treaty of 1921 undid it for most of the island.
