title: O'Connell and Catholic Emancipation
titleline: O'Connell and Catholic Emancipation - The History Web
para1: Catholic Emancipation. Daniel O'Connell was a Kerry lawyer, a brilliant barrister and a devout Catholic who believed revolutions were made in courts and meetings, not on battlefields. In 1823 he founded the Catholic Association with a stroke of genius: the Catholic Rent, a subscription of a penny a month that let the poorest cottier join. Within a few years the association had enrolled a mass membership counted in the millions, organized parish by parish through the priests, and turned the demand for Catholic Emancipation - the right of Catholics to sit in Parliament - into the first mass democratic movement in European history.
para2: The law said a Catholic could not take a seat in Parliament; it did not say one could not be elected. In 1828 O'Connell himself stood for County Clare against a sitting minister, and the forty-shilling freeholders - the small Catholic tenants, voting against their landlords' orders for the first time - elected him by a landslide. Ireland held its breath: if O'Connell was refused his seat, the prime minister, the Duke of Wellington, warned, the kingdom might face civil war.
para3: Wellington, the victor of Waterloo and no friend of concession, chose concession. With Robert Peel he forced the Roman Catholic Relief Act through Parliament in April 1829: Catholics could at last sit at Westminster, hold nearly all public offices, and vote on equal terms. It was the most consequential climbdown of the century - it split the Tory party for a generation - and it had been extorted not by violence but by the disciplined mobilization of an unarmed people.
para4: O'Connell took his seat as the Liberator, the uncrowned king of Ireland, and turned to his next cause: Repeal of the Union. His monster meetings of the 1840s drew crowds counted in the hundreds of thousands - at Tara in 1843 perhaps three-quarters of a million - until the government banned the Clontarf meeting, O'Connell backed down rather than risk blood, and his movement broke. He died in 1847, on pilgrimage to Rome, in the worst year of the Famine. His methods - mass organization, disciplined nonviolence, moral pressure - were studied by every later movement from Chartism to Gandhi.

title: The Great Famine
titleline: The Great Famine - The History Web
para1: The Great Famine. In September 1845 a strange blight appeared on the potato fields of Ireland - leaves blackened overnight, and the tubers in the ground turned to stinking pulp. Phytophthora infestans had come from America to Europe, and in Ireland it struck the one country where a third of the people ate almost nothing but potatoes: fourteen pounds a day for an adult laborer, with buttermilk, on plots too small for any other crop to sustain. The blight returned in 1846, worse, and again in 1848. The food of four million people simply ceased to exist.
para2: Hunger became starvation, and starvation brought the fevers - typhus and relapsing fever - that killed more than hunger did. The roads filled with walking skeletons; families were found dead in their cabins with grass in their mouths; workhouses overflowed and closed their gates. And all through it, Ireland - a food-exporting country under the same crown as the richest state on earth - shipped grain and livestock to England under guard. Relief came grudgingly: public works that paid a dying man wages to break stones, then soup kitchens that at their peak in 1847 fed three million people a day, then were closed and the burden thrown on the poor rates and the landlords.
para3: The landlords answered with eviction. Tens of thousands of families were turned out of their cabins, which were tumbled - unroofed - behind them to prevent return, and the crowded coffin ships carried the survivors to Liverpool, Quebec and New York, where fever followed them into the quarantine stations at Grosse Isle. The charitable effort, above all the Quakers', was heroic; the state's, in the judgment of its own relief commissioners and of posterity, was governed by dogma - that the market must not be interfered with, and that the Irish must be taught to stand alone.
para4: Between 1845 and 1852 about one million people died and more than a million emigrated, out of a population of eight and a half million; and the emigration did not stop - by 1924 Ireland's population had halved while every other country in Europe grew. The Famine emptied the west, killed the Irish language across whole counties, planted the Irish diaspora in America - and planted in that diaspora an undying hatred that would finance Fenians, fund Parnell, and arm the generation of 1916. It is the wound at the center of modern Irish history.

title: The Fenians and the Rising of 1867
titleline: The Fenians and the Rising of 1867 - The History Web
para1: The Fenians. Out of the Famine generation came men who concluded that Ireland would never be freed by meetings and petitions. In 1858 James Stephens in Dublin and John O'Mahony in New York founded a secret, oath-bound revolutionary brotherhood - the Irish Republican Brotherhood at home, the Fenian Brotherhood among the emigrants in America - dedicated to one end: an Irish republic, won by force of arms. They took their name from the Fianna, the warrior band of Irish legend, and they invented the model of the modern revolutionary underground: cell structure, secret oath, a newspaper, and money from the diaspora.
para2: Fenianism's strength was the Famine's legacy: hundreds of thousands of Irish in America, many of them fresh from the Union and Confederate armies, trained, armed and bitter. The movement dreamed of a war on two fronts - insurrection in Ireland, invasion of Canada from the United States. Fenian raiders actually crossed the Canadian border in 1866 and won a skirmish at Ridgeway before dispersing; in Ireland the brotherhood recruited deep into the British army itself, among the Irish soldiers of the garrison.
para3: The government struck first, sweeping up the leadership in 1865. The rising, when it finally came in March 1867, was a forlorn hope: scattered bands in Kerry, Limerick, Tipperary and Cork attacked police barracks in a late-winter blizzard and were scattered in days. What made the Fenians immortal was not the fighting but the aftermath - the Manchester Martyrs, three Fenians hanged in 1867 for a rescue in which a policeman was shot, and the Clerkenwell prison explosion that killed Londoners in the cause. God save Ireland, sung by the Manchester three at their trial, became the anthem of a movement.
para4: The rising failed, and Fenianism's violence split Irish opinion, but the tradition did not die: it became the backbone of physical-force republicanism, the ideology of 1916. And the Fenian scare had one great constitutional consequence - it convinced William Gladstone that Ireland's grievances were real, setting in train fifty years of reform: the disestablishment of the Irish church, the land acts, and at last Home Rule itself.

title: The Land War and Parnell
titleline: The Land War and Parnell - The History Web
para1: The Land War. Ireland in 1879 was a country of tenants: nearly all the land belonged to a few thousand landlords, mostly Protestant, many absentee, and the three million people who worked it had no legal right beyond the year's lease. When the harvest failed in 1879 and Famine memories woke, the west rose in a new kind of war - not for a republic this time, but for the land itself. The Irish National Land League, founded by Michael Davitt, a Fenian whose own family had been evicted, demanded the three Fs: fair rent, fixity of tenure, free sale.
para2: The Land League's weapon was organized non-cooperation, and its chief victim gave the English language a new word: Captain Charles Boycott, a Mayo land-agent against whom the League perfected the social and economic ostracism that became the boycott. The movement's parliamentary arm was led by Charles Stewart Parnell, the cold, magnetic Protestant landlord who became the uncrowned king of Ireland, holding the balance at Westminster with a disciplined Irish party and using obstruction to force Ireland onto the floor of the House of Commons.
para3: The government answered with coercion and the League answered with No-Rent manifestos; Parnell and Davitt were jailed in Kilmainham, and from prison came the Kilmainham Treaty of 1882: the prisoners released, the rent question settled by law. The pact was shaken within days by the Phoenix Park murders - the assassination of the new Chief Secretary by a splinter group - but the settlement held. Gladstone's Land Acts of 1881 and the later Wyndham Act of 1903 transformed Ireland: fair rents fixed by tribunals, then state-financed purchase, until the tenants of Ireland became owners of their farms.
para4: Parnell did not live to see it. At the height of his power, with Home Rule seemingly won, he was destroyed by the O'Shea divorce case of 1890; the party split into Parnellite and anti-Parnellite, and he died broken in 1891, aged forty-five. But the Land War had already done its work: it had broken the landlords, created the class of owner-occupier farmers who would be the backbone of the Irish state, and shown that disciplined mass organization could win what rebellions could not.

title: The Home Rule Crisis
titleline: The Home Rule Crisis - The History Web
para1: The Home Rule Crisis. Home Rule - an Irish parliament in Dublin for Irish affairs, within the United Kingdom - was the settled demand of constitutional nationalism from the 1870s, and twice it came within a breath of law. Gladstone's first bill fell in 1886, splitting his own party; his second passed the Commons in 1893 and was thrown out by the Lords. When the Parliament Act of 1911 broke the Lords' veto, a third Home Rule Bill was introduced in 1912, and this time nothing in the constitution could stop it. Ireland would have Home Rule by 1914 - unless someone stopped it by force.
para2: Ulster's Protestants resolved to stop it by force. Home Rule, they held, meant Rome Rule: a Dublin parliament would be a Catholic parliament, and the Protestant, industrial, unionist northeast would be submerged in a Catholic, agrarian Ireland. In September 1912 nearly half a million men and women signed the Solemn League and Covenant, pledging to resist by all means; in 1913 they raised the Ulster Volunteer Force, one hundred thousand strong, and in April 1914 they landed twenty-five thousand German rifles at Larne. The nationalists answered with the Irish Volunteers and their own gun-running at Howth. Ireland stood on the edge of civil war, and the British army itself wavered - in the Curragh incident, officers refused to move against Ulster.
para3: The question that could not be answered was Ulster itself: would the northeast be excluded from Home Rule, for six years or forever, four counties or nine? The Buckingham Palace Conference of July 1914 failed on exactly this point. Days later, Europe went to war, and Home Rule was enacted and suspended in the same breath, for the duration.
para4: The suspension killed constitutional nationalism. The Irish Volunteers split; the republican wing, seeing its chance in England's difficulty, went on to the Easter Rising of 1916, and the Ulster Volunteers marched instead to the Somme, where the 36th (Ulster) Division was bled white on the first day. When the war ended, the Home Rule Ireland of 1912 was dead: the demand now was a republic, and Ulster's answer would be partition.

title: The Easter Rising, 1916
titleline: The Easter Rising, 1916 - The History Web
para1: The Easter Rising. While the empire fought for its life in France, a handful of Irish republicans resolved to strike for a republic at home. The Irish Republican Brotherhood's military council - Tom Clarke, Sean MacDermott, Patrick Pearse, James Connolly, Joseph Plunkett, Eamonn Ceannt, Thomas MacDonagh - planned in secrecy even from their own movement's leadership, and German help, promised by Roger Casement, was lost at sea on Good Friday 1916. On Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, about twelve hundred men and women of the Irish Volunteers and Connolly's Citizen Army seized key buildings in Dublin, and Pearse stood on the steps of the General Post Office to read the Proclamation of the Irish Republic.
para2: The rising was militarily hopeless and the rebels knew it. For six days they held the GPO and a ring of posts around the city center against artillery, gunboats on the Liffey, and twenty thousand troops; the center of Dublin burned, and by the time Pearse surrendered on 29 April, some 450 people were dead - more than half of them civilians - and three thousand wounded. Dubliners jeered the prisoners as they were marched away; the rising seemed a futile gesture by a fringe.
para3: The executions transformed it. Between 3 and 12 May the British shot fifteen of the leaders, one by one, at Kilmainham Gaol: Pearse, Clarke, MacDermott, Connolly - wounded, shot tied to a chair - Plunkett, married in his cell hours before the firing party, and the rest. Ireland watched the men it had dismissed as cranks die like martyrs, and public opinion swung behind them. As Yeats wrote within the year, all changed, changed utterly: a terrible beauty is born.
para4: The rising remade Ireland. Sinn Fein, rebuilt on the martyrs' names, swept the election of 1918; the First Dail met in 1919; the War of Independence followed; and the Free State that emerged in 1922 was governed, for its first half-century, almost entirely by the men and women of Easter Week. The proclamation's dead signatories became the founding fathers of the Irish state - and its unfulfilled promises the measure of every Irish government since.

title: The Anglo-Irish War and the Irish Free State
titleline: The Anglo-Irish War and the Irish Free State - The History Web
para1: The Anglo-Irish War. In December 1918 Sinn Fein won three-quarters of Ireland's seats, and in January 1919 its elected members refused Westminster and met in Dublin as Dail Eireann, the parliament of the Irish Republic proclaimed in 1916. On the same day, in Tipperary, Volunteers shot dead two policemen escorting gelignite - the opening shots of a war no one had declared. Michael Collins, the Dail's director of intelligence, built the war's machinery: a flying column in every fighting county for ambush and guerrilla war, and in Dublin a squad and a network of spies that struck at the heart of British intelligence.
para2: The war was fought in the dark: the IRA burned barracks and ambushed patrols, the Crown forces - reinforced by the Black and Tans and the Auxiliaries, ex-soldiers turned loose as reprisal squads - answered with sacked towns and murdered suspects, from Croke Park on Bloody Sunday to the burning of Cork. It was ugly, intimate, and unwinnable for both sides: Britain could not reconquer Ireland without a full-scale war it had no stomach for, and the IRA could not fight much longer. In July 1921 both sides took the truce.
para3: The Treaty, signed in London in December 1921 by Collins and Griffith's delegation, gave Ireland dominion status as the Irish Free State - self-government like Canada's, with an oath of allegiance to the Crown, and with Northern Ireland, created by partition in 1921, free to opt out, which it did at once. Collins called it freedom to achieve freedom; de Valera and the republican diehards called it betrayal. The Dail approved it by seven votes, and the movement of Easter Week split in two.
para4: The split became civil war (1922-23), Free State against republican, brother against brother; Collins himself was killed in an ambush in his native Cork. The pro-Treaty side won, at the price of executions harsher than anything the British had done in 1916, and built the state: within the decade the Free State was a functioning democracy, and the Free State was already finding its own course within the Commonwealth. The war of 1919-21 had won for twenty-six counties the independence that six centuries of conquest had refused - at the price of partition and a fratricide whose shadows still lay long.

title: Tudor England: Henry VII and Henry VIII
titleline: Tudor England: Henry VII and Henry VIII - The History Web
para1: Tudor England. The Tudors were an accident of war. Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, had a distant claim to the throne and a small army of French mercenaries when he landed in Wales in 1485; at Bosworth Field he killed Richard III and took the crown as Henry VII, ending the Wars of the Roses. The new dynasty was illegitimate in half the kingdom's eyes, and Henry VII spent his reign making it safe: marrying Elizabeth of York to join the warring roses, hunting down pretenders like Lambert Simnel and Perkin Warbeck, and filling his treasury by extortionate but peaceable government. He left his son a full exchequer and an unchallenged crown.
para2: Henry VIII inherited in 1509: young, rich, magnificent, and determined to cut a figure in Europe. For twenty years his reign was governed by Cardinal Wolsey and remembered for pageantry - the Field of the Cloth of Gold - and for the burning question that consumed it: the King's Great Matter, his demand to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, who had given him a daughter, Mary, but no living son. When the Pope refused, Henry broke with Rome.
para3: The English Reformation was made by statute, in a single revolutionary decade. Between 1532 and 1534 Henry's Parliament cut every tie to Rome and declared the king Supreme Head of the Church of England; Thomas More and John Fisher died on the scaffold rather than swear it. Thomas Cromwell then engineered the dissolution of the monasteries - eight hundred religious houses closed, their lands sold to the gentry, their shrines stripped - a transfer of a fifth of England's land and a blow from which the old church never recovered. Henry married six wives in all, executed two of them, and fathered the three children who would rule after him.
para4: The break with Rome was Henry's, but its consequences ran far beyond him: England was launched on its path as a Protestant power, its navy - Henry's own creation, with its great ships and dockyards - was the seed of sea power, and the crown stood stronger than ever. When Henry died in 1547, the England of his children's reigns - Edward's zealous Protestantism, Mary's fires, Elizabeth's long settlement - had been set on its course by his monumental self-will.

title: Elizabethan England and the Spanish Armada
titleline: Elizabethan England and the Spanish Armada - The History Web
para1: Elizabethan England. Elizabeth I came to the throne in 1558 after the traumas of her siblings' reigns - her brother Edward's radical Protestantism, her sister Mary's Catholic restoration and the burning of heretics - and she ruled for forty-five years, the longest and most storied reign England had known. Her first work was the Elizabethan Settlement: a Church of England Protestant in doctrine but broad enough, she hoped, to hold a divided nation. Her next was survival: excommunicated by the Pope, plotted against by her Catholic subjects in the name of her cousin Mary, Queen of Scots - whom she kept prisoner for nineteen years and at last, in 1587, reluctantly sent to the block.
para2: Elizabeth's England lived by the sea. Merchants and sea-dogs - Drake, Hawkins, Raleigh, Frobisher - pushed English ships into the trades Spain claimed as its own: Drake's circumnavigation (1577-1580) came home laden with Spanish treasure, and his raids on the Caribbean and Cadiz were licensed piracy that filled the queen's coffers. In 1588 Philip II of Spain, exasperated by the raids, the execution of Mary, and English aid to his Dutch rebels, sent the Great Armada: one hundred and thirty ships to escort an invasion army from the Netherlands. In the Channel fights and at Gravelines the faster English gunnery ships harried it, fireships broke its formation, and the weather did the rest; half the Armada was lost on the coasts of Scotland and Ireland.
para3: The defeat of the Armada made Elizabeth a legend - she had ridden to Tilbury to tell her army she had the heart and stomach of a king - and it opened the great age of English confidence. These were the years of Shakespeare's plays, Marlowe, Spenser's Faerie Queene, the madrigal and the miniature; of London doubling in size; of grammar schools, of voyages to Virginia and the East, of a nation intensely aware of itself.
para4: The last decade darkened: the long, ruinous war in Ireland, Essex's rebellion, bad harvests and the queen's own fading. She died in 1603, childless by design - I am married to England - and the crown passed peacefully to her Scottish Stuart cousin. The Elizabethan age fixed England's self-image for four hundred years: Protestant, maritime, and defying the great powers of the continent.

title: The Union of the Crowns, 1603
titleline: The Union of the Crowns, 1603 - The History Web
para1: The Union of the Crowns. In the last hour of 24 March 1603 Elizabeth I died at Richmond, and before dawn Sir Robert Carey was riding hard for Scotland with the news. At Holyrood, King James VI of Scots - son of Mary, Queen of Scots, and great-great-grandson of Henry VII - learned that he was now James I of England as well. It was the union England and Scotland had fought over for three hundred years, achieved in an instant by inheritance: the crowns of the two ancient enemies joined on one head, and the Stuart dynasty seated in London.
para2: James rode south to a rapturous welcome and quickly found that two crowns were not one kingdom. He proposed himself King of Great Britain and asked both parliaments for a full union - one law, one church settlement, free trade, one citizenship. Both refused: England would not share its laws or its trade with the poorer Scots, and Scotland would not be absorbed. The union of 1603 remained personal, not political: two kingdoms, two parliaments, two established churches, one king. James had to content himself with a flag - the first Union Jack - and a Bible, the King James Version of 1611, sponsored to bind his two peoples in one scripture.
para3: The divided inheritance stored up trouble. The Stuarts were now absentee kings of Scotland, governing it through bishops and favorites from London, and absentee landlords of Irish plantations. The attempt of James's son Charles I to force English-style worship on Presbyterian Scotland would provoke the Bishops' Wars, and the Bishops' Wars would light the fuse of the English Civil War: the three kingdoms could no longer be pulled apart, and they dragged one another into the wars of the 1640s.
para4: Still, 1603 settled the great question of the island: never again would England and Scotland make war as sovereign enemies. For a century the union of crowns worked awkwardly, until the Act of Union of 1707 made it a union of parliaments - and the kingdom James had wanted, Great Britain, finally came into being.

title: The Restoration
titleline: The Restoration - The History Web
para1: The Restoration. When Oliver Cromwell died in 1658, the republic he had built on the ruins of monarchy died with him. His son Richard could not hold it; the army and the Parliament tore at each other, and England, sick of soldiers and saints, remembered that it had once had a king. General George Monck marched his army down from Scotland, forced elections, and in April 1660 the new Convention Parliament received a letter from exile: the Declaration of Breda, in which Charles II promised pardon, religious liberty and payment of the army. On 29 May 1660, his thirtieth birthday, Charles entered London through crowds gone half-mad with joy. The monarchy was restored.
para2: The Restoration was a settlement as much as a celebration. The Convention confirmed the land-purchases of the revolution years - the republic's buyers kept their acres - and punished only the regicides, the men who had signed his father's death warrant, exhuming Cromwell's corpse to hang it. But the restored Cavalier Parliament took its own revenge on the Puritans: the Clarendon Code drove dissenting clergy from their pulpits and meeting-houses, and the theaters reopened with a wit and license that made Restoration comedy a byword.
para3: Charles II ruled twenty-five years by charm, cunning and French gold. His reign endured the Great Plague of 1665 and the Great Fire of London of 1666, the shock of the Dutch fleet burning his ships in the Medway, the fabricated terror of the Popish Plot, and the great constitutional fight of the Exclusion Crisis, when Parliament tried to bar his Catholic brother James from the throne and lost. Charles ruled his last four years without a parliament at all - and died, in 1685, received into the Catholic Church on his deathbed.
para4: The Restoration settled the terms on which England would be governed: monarchy yes, absolutism no. Charles never forgot that his brother would lose the throne in three years for the sins his father had died for; when James II provoked his own overthrow in 1688, the kingdom removed him without a civil war. Merry, cynical, careful Charles had taught the monarchy how to survive in the world Parliament had made.

title: Georgian Britain and the Regency
titleline: Georgian Britain and the Regency - The History Web
para1: Georgian Britain. The four Georges ruled from 1714 to 1830, and under them Britain became the first industrial nation and the greatest commercial power on earth. The dynasty began precariously: George I was a German Lutheran of Hanover, fifty-fourth in the ordinary line, brought in by the Act of Settlement to keep the Catholic Stuarts out. He spoke little English and cared more for Hanover, and the consequences were constitutional: as the king withdrew from the cabinet, power passed to his ministers - to Sir Robert Walpole, who governed for twenty years and is counted the first Prime Minister.
para2: The dynasty survived the Stuart counterattacks - the Jacobite risings of 1715 and 1745 - and under George III, who gloried in the name of Briton, the monarchy re-engaged. George III's sixty-year reign (1760-1820) held most of the age's dramas: the loss of the American colonies, the long wars against revolutionary and Napoleonic France won at sea by Nelson and on land by Wellington, the union with Ireland in 1801, and the king's own tragedy - the madness, now thought to be porphyria, that from 1811 left his son ruling as Prince Regent.
para3: It was an age of astonishing surface. Georgian Britain gave the world the Georgian terrace and the crescent - Bath, Edinburgh's New Town, Regency London under Nash - the novels of Jane Austen, the poetry of Byron and Wordsworth, the landscapes of Constable and Turner, the science of the Royal Society, and a political world of rotten boroughs, coffee-house debate and savage caricature. Beneath the elegance ran hunger, gin, the press-gang, and the new industrial towns where the future was being forged.
para4: The Regency ended in the Brighton Pavilion splendor of George IV; his brother William IV presided over the Great Reform Act of 1832; and in 1837 the crown passed to the eighteen-year-old Victoria. The Georgian age had carried Britain from a minor Protestant kingdom to the workshop and the ruler of the world's seas - and left the monarchy transformed from a governing power into a national symbol.

title: The Industrial Revolution
titleline: The Industrial Revolution - The History Web
para1: The Industrial Revolution. Between about 1760 and 1840, in a corner of an island off Europe, human beings escaped the oldest prison of their species: the limit of what muscle, wind and water could do. The Industrial Revolution began in Britain for reasons that converged nowhere else: cheap coal at the surface, high wages that made machines worth building, ironmasters and tinkerers in a tolerant scientific culture, an empire's markets, a navy to reach them, and a state that let inventors keep their profits.
para2: It began in cotton. The flying shuttle, Hargreaves's spinning jenny, Arkwright's water frame, Crompton's mule - within a generation, the spinning and weaving of cotton moved from the cottage to the mill, and Manchester grew from a town into Cottonopolis, the first industrial city. Then came the master key: James Watt's improved steam engine, built with Matthew Boulton from 1776, which freed the factory from the riverbank and put rotary power anywhere coal could be carried. Coal, iron and steam became the trinity of the new economy; Abraham Darby's coke-smelted iron at Coalbrookdale built the world's first iron bridge in 1779.
para3: The canals cut in the 1760s, then the macadam and Telford roads, and finally the railway - Stockton to Darlington in 1825, Liverpool to Manchester in 1830, where Stephenson's Rocket proved the locomotive - shrank the country and annihilated distance. By 1850 Britain produced half the world's iron and half its cotton cloth, carried most of its trade, and at the Great Exhibition of 1851, in Paxton's Crystal Palace, displayed itself without irony as the workshop of the world.
para4: The human price was paid in the mill towns: children in the spinning rooms, the cholera cities Engels described, the ten-hour day fought for decade by decade. And yet the transformation was total and irreversible: by 1851 more Britons lived in towns than in the country - the first people in history to do so. What began in the Midlands valleys spread to Belgium, Germany, America and the world, and changed the conditions of ordinary life beyond anything conquest had ever done.

title: Victorian Britain
titleline: Victorian Britain - The History Web
para1: Victorian Britain. Victoria was eighteen when she came to the throne in 1837, and she reigned sixty-three years - so long that her name became an adjective for an entire civilization. At her accession Britain was the first industrial power; at her death in 1901 it governed a quarter of mankind and produced a third of the world's manufactures. The Victorian age was the zenith of British power and self-confidence, the age of the Great Exhibition, of the largest navy, the widest empire, and the City of London as the bank of the world.
para2: It was also an age of relentless change at home. The railway net, the telegraph, the penny post and the daily newspaper bound the kingdom together; the great cities - London, Glasgow, Manchester, Birmingham - became the largest on earth; and the franchise widened by stages, in 1832, 1867 and 1884, until most men could vote. The state slowly learned to govern an industrial society: the Factory Acts, the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846, the public health acts after the cholera years, free elementary education in 1870.
para3: Victoria herself, with Prince Albert, remade the monarchy into the nation's family - a pattern of duty and domesticity that outlasted her. Beneath the confident surface ran the age's anxieties: the condition of the poor in the East End and the potteries, the Irish question rising toward Home Rule, and from the 1870s the first challengers - a unified Germany and an expanding America - overtaking British industry. The empire reached its ceremonial height in the Diamond Jubilee of 1897; the Boer War, beginning two years later, showed the strain.
para4: She died at Osborne in January 1901, and the world she left was recognizably the modern one: urban, literate, industrial, democratic in tendency, and girdled by British cables and British ships. The twentieth century's wars would test that inheritance; the Victorians' works - the sewers, railways, parliaments and institutions - still carry the weight of British life.

title: Chartism and the Reform Acts
titleline: Chartism and the Reform Acts - The History Web
para1: Chartism and the Reform Acts. In 1832 the Great Reform Act redrew the political map of Britain: the rotten boroughs were swept away, the industrial cities got seats, and the vote went to the middle class. But the working men who had marched and petitioned for the act got nothing, and their answer came in 1838: the People's Charter, six demands for full democracy - a vote for every man, the secret ballot, no property qualification for MPs, payment of members, equal constituencies, and annual parliaments. Chartism was born, the first mass working-class political movement in the world.
para2: Three times the Chartists carried monster petitions to Parliament - in 1839 with over a million signatures, in 1842 with more than three million, in 1848 with what they claimed were six million - and three times Parliament refused to look at them. The movement strained between its prophets: William Lovett's moral force of education and self-improvement, and Feargus O'Connor's physical force that flirted with insurrection. In 1839 a rising of Welsh miners at Newport was shot down; in 1842 the general strike of the Plug Plots swept the mill towns; in 1848, with Europe in revolution, the government swore in two hundred thousand special constables - and the Kennington Common meeting dispersed in the rain.
para3: Chartism died of its failures and of prosperity: the repeal of the Corn Laws, the rising wages of the 1850s, and emigration drew off its force, and its last leader, O'Connor, ended his days in an asylum. The ruling classes congratulated themselves that England was not a revolutionary country.
para4: And then, peacefully and by degrees, the Charter won. The secret ballot came in 1872, payment of MPs in 1911; the Second Reform Act of 1867 doubled the electorate and gave town working men the vote, the Third in 1884 extended it to the counties, and by 1918 nearly every man - and the first women - had the vote. Five of the Charter's six points are the law of the land today; only annual parliaments were never tried. Chartism lost every battle and won the war for British democracy.

title: Britain in the First World War
titleline: Britain in the First World War - The History Web
para1: Britain in the First World War. On 4 August 1914, after Germany invaded Belgium, Britain declared war. The small professional army - the Old Contemptibles of the British Expeditionary Force - crossed the Channel at once and was nearly destroyed holding the line at Mons, Le Cateau and the first Battle of Ypres. Kitchener's call for volunteers answered the loss: by 1916 nearly two and a half million men had enlisted, many in the Pals battalions where streets, factories and football teams joined together - and would die together.
para2: The war in the trenches consumed them. The first day of the Somme, 1 July 1916, was the worst day in the history of the British army: nearly twenty thousand dead before noon, among them the 36th (Ulster) Division and the Newfoundland Regiment, for gains measured in yards. Loos, Arras, Passchendaele followed - battles of mud, wire and machine guns that became permanent words in the language of grief. Yet the army of 1918 that finally broke the German line in the Hundred Days was the most powerful Britain ever fielded, and at sea the blockade and Jutland held the ring.
para3: The home front was remade as thoroughly as the army. Lloyd George's munitions ministry organized an economy of total war; women - over a million of them - went into the shell factories and onto the buses and the land, work that helped win them the vote in 1918; conscription, rationing and DORA's censorship reached into every home. Ireland convulsed in the Easter Rising of 1916, and in 1918 Britain fought its election on the promise to make a land fit for heroes.
para4: Victory came on 11 November 1918 at a price the country could not count: some 880,000 British dead, two million wounded, a national debt multiplied tenfold, and in nearly every town and village a war memorial with too many names. The empire stood at its greatest extent - and its foundations were cracked. Britain after 1918 was poorer, more democratic, less certain, and shadowed by the generation that had not come home.

title: Mary Queen of Scots and the Scottish Reformation
titleline: Mary Queen of Scots and the Scottish Reformation - The History Web
para1: Mary Queen of Scots. She was six days old when her father James V died in 1542 and she became Queen of Scots. Raised at the glittering French court and married briefly to the King of France, the tall, beautiful, Catholic Mary returned in 1561 to a Scotland she barely knew - a cold, poor kingdom in the grip of the Reformation, where John Knox thundered against her mass from the pulpit of St Giles. For six years she ruled with real political skill, governing with her Protestant half-brother Moray and her Protestant council while practicing her own faith in private.
para2: Her private life destroyed her. The marriage to her cousin Henry Darnley gave her an heir - the future James VI - and a feckless, vicious husband who murdered her secretary Rizzio at her supper table. Darnley himself was strangled at Kirk o' Field in February 1567; three months later Mary married the man everyone believed his murderer, the Earl of Bothwell. The scandal broke her authority completely: the lords rose, her army melted at Carberry Hill, and she was forced to abdicate in favor of her baby son. In 1568 she escaped, lost the battle of Langside, and rode across the Solway into England - into what she thought was sanctuary and was in fact a nineteen-year imprisonment.
para3: Meanwhile Scotland was remade without her. The Reformation Parliament of 1560 had abolished the mass and the Pope's authority, and Knox's Kirk - Calvinist, governed by presbyteries, devoted to a school in every parish - became the national church of a nation that learned to read its Bible. Mary's son James was raised a Protestant king. The Scottish Reformation, unlike England's, came from below and against the crown's will, and it made Scotland a different country: kirk session, catechism and the godly commonwealth.
para4: Mary in captivity became the hope of every Catholic plot against Elizabeth, and in 1586 the Babington Plot gave her jailers their evidence. She was tried, condemned, and beheaded at Fotheringhay in February 1587, meeting death with a courage that fixed her legend. The last irony was hers: in 1603 her son inherited Elizabeth's throne, and Mary's line, not her jailer's, rules the British Isles to this day.

title: The Covenanters
titleline: The Covenanters - The History Web
para1: The Covenanters. In 1637 Charles I and his archbishop, William Laud, imposed a new English-style prayer book on Presbyterian Scotland. When it was first read in St Giles' Cathedral in Edinburgh, tradition says a market-woman named Jenny Geddes threw her stool at the minister's head - and Scotland rose. In February 1638 the nation signed the National Covenant: a bond, sworn by nobles, ministers, merchants and ploughmen on their knees in Greyfriars Kirkyard and in every parish, to defend the Presbyterian Kirk against royal interference. The Covenanters would tolerate no king between a Scot and his God.
para2: Covenanting Scotland beat its king. In the Bishops' Wars of 1639-40 the Army of the Covenant out-marched and out-organized Charles's levies, and in 1640 a Scottish army occupied Newcastle and dictated terms. The king's weakness summoned the English Parliament that would fight the Civil War - and in 1643 the Covenanters joined it, sending an army south under the Solemn League and Covenant, which helped win Marston Moor. But when the English revolution devoured itself and executed Charles in 1649, the horrified Covenanters crowned his son - and Cromwell came north to destroy their armies at Dunbar and Worcester's forerunner at Inverkeithing.
para3: At the Restoration, Charles II had his revenge: episcopacy was reimposed, and the ministers who refused it were driven from their parishes to preach at open-air conventicles in the hills. The later Stuart persecution - the Killing Time of the 1680s - hunted the field-preachers with dragoons; the Cameronians of the southwest answered with arms and martyrdom. The names of the martyrs, and the graves in the kirkyards of Galloway, entered the memory of Presbyterian Scotland and Presbyterian Ulster, where thousands of Scots carried the Covenant across the water.
para4: The Glorious Revolution of 1688 ended the struggle: in 1690 the Scottish Parliament abolished bishops forever and established the Presbyterian Church of Scotland, which endures as the national church. The Covenanters' stubborn theology left a double legacy - a democratic kirk governed from below, and a tradition of conscience against power that echoed far beyond Scotland, in Ulster and in America.

title: The Jacobite Risings
titleline: The Jacobite Risings - The History Web
para1: The Jacobite Risings. When the Catholic James VII and II was driven from his thrones in 1688, his cause - Jacobitism, from Jacobus, Latin for James - refused to die. For sixty years the exiled Stuarts plotted their return from France and Rome, and their most loyal army was the Highlands of Scotland, where the clan chiefs kept the old faith, the old feuds, and a feudal levy of broadsword and targe. The risings came in waves: Killiecrankie in 1689, where Dundee's clans won and died; then, after the Union of 1707 doubled Scotland's discontents, the great attempts.
para2: The Fifteen (1715) rose for James VIII, the Old Pretender: the Earl of Mar raised the clans, fought a draw at Sheriffmuir, and let the moment die before James even landed. The Forty-Five was the romantic last throw: in July 1745 Charles Edward Stuart - Bonnie Prince Charlie - landed in the Hebrides with seven companions, raised his father's standard at Glenfinnan, and led a Highland army to a stunning victory at Prestonpans, took Edinburgh, and in December marched into England as far as Derby, one hundred and twenty miles from London, with the capital in panic.
para3: At Derby the chiefs forced the retreat - no English Jacobites had risen, and two armies lay between them and London. The clans fell back north through the winter, and on 16 April 1746, on the flat moor of Culloden near Inverness, five thousand hungry Highlanders charged into the muskets and cannon of the Duke of Cumberland's army. It was over in an hour; the wounded were finished where they lay. Charles wandered five months in the heather, sheltered by Flora MacDonald and the poorest of the poor, and escaped to France and a long, sodden exile.
para4: The state answered Culloden with the destruction of the world that had made it: the Disarming Act, the banning of tartan and bagpipes, the abolition of heritable jurisdictions - the chief's power of life and death - and garrisons and roads driven into the glens. Jacobitism died, and within a generation the same Highlands supplied the British army its most famous regiments; the tartan came back as pageantry for George IV's Edinburgh visit in 1822, staged by Walter Scott. The rising of the clans had failed - and conquered the world's imagination.

title: The Highland Clearances
titleline: The Highland Clearances - The History Web
para1: The Highland Clearances. In the generations after Culloden, the chiefs of the Scottish Highlands - shorn of their old powers, schooled in the south, and deep in the debts of lowland fashion - discovered that their glens were worth more grazed by sheep than farmed by men. The Cheviot and the Blackface could pay rents the small tenants, the crofters, could not. So, beginning in the late eighteenth century and running for a hundred years, the people of the Highlands were cleared: moved off the inland townships where their families had farmed since before memory, to make way for the great sheep walks.
para2: The worst of it was on the Sutherland estates, where between 1807 and 1821 the agents of the Countess of Sutherland - Patrick Sellar above all - removed some fifteen thousand people, burning the roof-timbers of the townships over the evicted so they could not return. Some families were offered tiny crofts on the barren coast, to live by fishing and kelp-burning; thousands more took ship for Canada, or were assisted - and sometimes forced - aboard by landlords glad to see them go. The people burned out of Strathnaver carried the name of Sellar's clearances, and of the duchess's, in bitterness for generations.
para3: The potato famine of 1846 brought a second, crueler wave: with the kelp trade dead and the crofts unable to feed them, the congested western glens and islands were cleared again - by eviction, by assisted emigration to Canada and Australia, and by simple destitution. The Highlands emptied: a region that had held a tenth of Scotland's people became a land of empty glens, deer forests for southern sportsmen, and ruins. Gaels called it na daoine a' dol as - the people going away.
para4: Resistance came late but came: the crofters' war of the 1880s - the Battle of the Braes, the rent strikes of Skye and Lewis - forced the Crofters' Holdings Act of 1886, which gave the remaining crofters secure tenure at last. The diaspora did the rest of the remembering: the cleared Highlanders peopled Glengarry, Nova Scotia and a hundred townships beyond, and the Clearances remain, for Scotland and for the Gaelic world, the great unhealed injury of its modern history.

title: The Scottish Enlightenment
titleline: The Scottish Enlightenment - The History Web
para1: The Scottish Enlightenment. In the half-century after 1740, poor, Presbyterian, post-Union Scotland produced an explosion of genius out of proportion to any nation in modern history. David Hume wrote the most searching philosophy in the language from his Edinburgh rooms; Adam Smith, a Glasgow professor, published the Wealth of Nations in 1776 and founded economics; Adam Ferguson invented sociology; William Robertson wrote the histories read across Europe; James Hutton founded geology; Joseph Black founded modern chemistry; and James Watt, a Glasgow instrument-maker, gave the industrial age its engine.
para2: It had institutions behind the genius. The Scottish universities - Edinburgh, Glasgow, Aberdeen, St Andrews - were cheap, open to talent, and taught in English rather than Latin, drawing students from England, Ireland and America. The parish school system, the Reformation's promise of a school in every parish, gave Scotland the highest literacy in Europe. And the Union of 1707, by removing politics to London, turned Scottish energy into inquiry: in the clubs of Edinburgh - the Select Society, the Poker Club - lawyers, ministers, doctors and lairds argued out the science of man.
para3: The Edinburgh they argued in became the Athens of the North: the New Town rising in neoclassical stone, the Encyclopaedia Britannica first published there in 1768, the Edinburgh Review setting the intellectual tone of the English-speaking world. From Edinburgh and Glasgow the Scottish idea traveled: to the American founding fathers, to the French economists, to every country where the modern sciences of society, wealth and the earth were taking shape.
para4: The Enlightenment's own terms defined the modern questions: Hume's skepticism, Smith's markets and moral sentiments, Hutton's deep time. Its legacy is so completely woven into modern thought that it is invisible - but for one astonishing century, the light of the world came from the wynds of Edinburgh and the college courts of Glasgow.

title: Industrial Wales: Coal, Iron and Slate
titleline: Industrial Wales: Coal, Iron and Slate - The History Web
para1: Industrial Wales. In 1750 Wales was a land of hill farmers; by 1900 it was one of the great workshops of the industrial world. The transformation began with iron: in 1759 the Dowlais works were founded at Merthyr Tydfil, where ironstone, coal, limestone and water power lay side by side, and within two generations Merthyr - a village become a town of furnaces, the largest in Wales - was the iron capital of the world. The Guest, Crawshay and Homfray works armed the wars against Napoleon, and Henry Cort's puddling process, developed for the Welsh works, made wrought iron by the shipload.
para2: Then came coal. The South Wales coalfield, from Pontypool to Milford Haven, held the finest steam coal on earth, and the navies and railways of the world steamed on Welsh coal. The valleys filled: the Rhondda, a scattering of farms in 1850, held 150,000 people by 1914, strung along terraces between the pitheads. Cardiff, a small port in 1801, became by 1913 the greatest coal-exporting harbor on earth, where the price of world coal was fixed in its Coal Exchange. In the northwest the slate quarries of Bethesda and Blaenau Ffestiniog roofed the cities of three continents.
para3: The wealth had its price, paid in the pits: Senghenydd in 1913, where 439 men and boys died in Britain's worst mining disaster, was one entry in a long ledger of explosion, flood and black lung. The valleys answered with their own institutions: the chapel, the eisteddfod, the male voice choir, the Workmen's Institutes and their libraries, and a fierce labor politics - the Tonypandy riots of 1910, the rise of the miners' unions, and eventually the Labour Party itself, which the valleys made their own for a century.
para4: Industrial Wales made a new Welsh identity, English-speaking in the valleys, Welsh-speaking in the slate country, confident and nonconformist. The boom could not last: after 1918 the coalfield entered its long decline, and the interwar valleys knew unemployment of a kind that scarred generations. But the age of coal and iron had transformed a rural nation into an industrial one, and the terraces, the tips and the hymns remain its monuments.
